title: Structural Limits of Privacy Protection: Why Contextual Integrity Cannot Be Automated

detail.title: Structural Limits of Privacy Protection: Why Contextual Integrity Cannot Be Automated
detail.abstract: This article identifies a fundamental constraint in automated privacy protection in cross-contextual settings where boundaries are constituted by non-disclosure. Modern data processing systems make billions of crosscontextual decisions hourly such as ad deliveries, content rankings, risk assessments, at a scale that precludes case-by-case human review, making the question of whether privacy can be protected within automated infrastructure practically urgent. We formalise the positive data constraint: the limitation lies not in what algorithms can compute but in what information reaches systems in the first place. Systems processing only observable data cannot detect boundaries users establish through deliberate non-disclosure. When Sacha engages with pregnancy content in magazines but withholds such engagement from social media, she establishes a contextual boundary through absence, that is, information no algorithm can systematically observe. Even Nissenbaum's implementation heuristic assumes observable contexts and flows, yet her unresolved Caller ID example reveals context ambiguity systems cannot resolve. We develop a three-hurdle framework mapping the boundary of automated data protection: (1) Observability: systems cannot detect information users withhold; (2) Relevance: systems can verify decisions use relevant data; (3) Inference revelation: systems can partially manage disclosure harms. Recognising this enables more effective protection: relevance baselines and revelation safeguards that systems can enforce, combined with human judgement and categorical prohibitions where they cannot. The framework provides a foundation for calibrating regulatory requirements to computational possibilities rather than aspirational standards no algorithm can satisfy.

title: Work From Home and Firm Productivity: The Role of ICT and Size
affiliations: London School of Economics, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Geography and Environment and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Geography and Environment

detail.title: Work From Home and Firm Productivity: The Role of ICT and Size
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the causal effect of work from home (WFH) adoption on firm productivity in the post-pandemic period. Using administrative firm-level data covering the universe of remote workers in Italy, we leverage exogenous pre-pandemic variation in firms’ access to fibre broadband as an instrument for WFH adoption. We find that WFH had a sizeable negative short-term impact on productivity, while larger firms and those with prior ICT investments mitigated these losses. In the longer term, the average effect of WFH is no longer statistically significant, though we find suggestive evidence of gains in firms with more postgraduate-educated employees.

title: Mechanistic Steering of Low-Variance Subspaces for Improved Factual Calibration in Large Language Models
affiliations: and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Mechanistic Steering of Low-Variance Subspaces for Improved Factual Calibration in Large Language Models
detail.abstract: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in high-stakes extraction tasks is limited by stochastic hallucination. We investigate the hypothesis that specific low-variance activation subspaces-systematically suppressed by Layer Normalization-encode latent signals of epistemic uncertainty. Utilizing Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on hidden states from a 32Bparameter transformer, we identify a 10-dimensional "dark" manifold where activation variance correlates with factual inconsistency. We propose an inference-time intervention, "Subspace Steering," which projects hidden states into this manifold to modulate model confidence. Our experiments observe a 12.1% absolute reduction in hallucination rates (from 14.2% to 2.1%) on a specialized legal-tech benchmark and a significant improvement in calibration-based abstention. We provide ablation studies comparing our method against random subspace steering, confirming the specific utility of the identified dark manifold.

title: Gen(X)AI: Boosting Explainable Artificial Intelligence for All
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), Peking University - HSBC School of Business, The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) and University of Colorado Denver

detail.title: Gen(X)AI: Boosting Explainable Artificial Intelligence for All
detail.abstract: As AI becomes increasingly embedded in organizational decision processes, the need for effective explanations of algorithmic outputs grows critical. Existing explainable AI (XAI) approaches emphasize technical transparency through visual feature attribution, yet these methods often fail to support meaningful human interpretation. We introduce GenXAI, a conversational explanation layer that translates model outputs into interactive natural-language explanations. Drawing on Cognitive Fit Theory and Construal Level Theory, we argue that explanation effectiveness depends on alignment between linguistic explanation style and the cognitive demands of decision tasks. Across two randomized experiments using a loan default prediction task, we show that conversational GenAI explanations significantly improve users' understanding of algorithmic predictions and decision confidence relative to static XAI visualizations. A second experiment isolates the mechanism by manipulating explanation style: concrete explanations—characterized by numerical specificity, benchmark comparisons, and structured reasoning—produce stronger improvements than abstract narrative explanations. Behavioral telemetry from chatbot interactions reveals that users exposed to concrete explanations process information more efficiently while spending more time deliberating, a pattern consistent with active reasoning rather than passive AI reliance. These findings advance XAI research by demonstrating that explanation effectiveness depends not only on technical transparency but on representational alignment between explanation style and task cognition. More broadly, the study highlights linguistic explanation design as a critical lever in conversational AI systems. For practice, organizations can improve human oversight of AI by complementing static transparency dashboards with conversational explanations that enable users to interrogate model reasoning.

title: The New Financial Lockdown: Inside India’s Account Freezing Regime
affiliations: Delhi High Court and Delhi High Court

detail.title: The New Financial Lockdown: Inside India’s Account Freezing Regime
detail.abstract: The transition from the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) has fundamentally reshaped the exercise of investigative powers, bringing the procedural intricacies of bank account freezing under Section 106 (erstwhile Section 102 CrPC) into sharp focus. This article provides a critical examination of the burgeoning "financial lockdown" caused by the mechanical and often disproportionate freezing of accounts by cybercrime units across India, a practice that frequently paralyses the financial lives of innocent individuals and businesses without a direct nexus to any alleged offence. It highlights a troubling systemic trend where agencies resort to informal "debit freezes" via the NCRP portal, bypassing mandatory statutory safeguards such as the recording of objective satisfaction and the immediate reporting of seizures to the jurisdictional Magistrate. By navigating through the jurisdictional vacuum that often leaves citizens without a timely remedy, the discourse argues that these arbitrary actions constitute a grave infringement of the fundamental rights to equality, trade, and livelihood guaranteed under Articles 14, 19(1)(g), and 21 of the Constitution of India. Drawing upon a comprehensive analysis of landmark precedents including the Supreme Court’s ruling in Shento Varghese (2024) and the mandates in Yashwant Singh and Neelkanth Pharma the piece explores the judicial shift towards the Principle of Proportionality, advocating for "Lien Marking" limited strictly to the disputed amount over blanket account restrictions. Ultimately, the analysis asserts that while investigative efficacy is paramount in the digital era, it must remain anchored in strict procedural discipline and proactive judicial oversight to ensure that preventive measures do not transform into extra-judicial punishment without due process.

title: Cognitive Twins: From Digital Representation to Governed Action

detail.title: Cognitive Twins: From Digital Representation to Governed Action
detail.abstract:
Complex organizations rely on fragmented decision systems that create coordination overhead, diffuse accountability, and difficulty scaling institutional knowledge. AI governance frameworks specify desired outcomes but leave open how those outcomes are enforced at runtime. This paper defines the Cognitive Twin, a decision-capable digital representation that executes a continuous G-PAPA decision cycle (Governance, Perception, Assembly, Prediction, Action). Governance is the defining property: embedded policy separates what the system can do from what it is authorized to do, and that separation is enforced at every subsequent step. Perception produces Observations under source-authority and quality constraints. Assembly processes admitted Observations to maintain a continuously updated world model of the managed entity. Prediction determines what is significant in the assembled state and forecasts how conditions may evolve. Action optimizes across competing objectives and, where authorized, executes. A Cognitive Twin provides a unified governed alternative to fragmented systems by maintaining persistent state, processing the full decision cycle, and enforcing explicit authority boundaries throughout. The paper contributes (i) a definition with five qualifying criteria, (ii) distinctions from related system types, and (iii) a governance-first architecture implemented as a network of Precision Agents with explicit policy checkpoints and auditable provenance. The goal is a precise specification for action-capable systems that remain accountable to institutional constraints.

title: Algorithmic Advice, Human Review, and Shared Liability
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business

detail.title: Algorithmic Advice, Human Review, and Shared Liability
detail.abstract: Algorithmic advice is often used not only to guide decisions but also to determine whether cases are escalated for costly review. I study advice design at deployment for an algorithm provider that observes a calibrated internal score and sends advice to a human decision maker who retains final authority, can pay to open review, and shares misclassification losses with the provider. A startup cost of review makes advice part of the escalation rule: optimal advice design targets the posterior beliefs at which review switches on or off, rather than preserving fine distinctions across the score distribution. This endogenous coarsening can pool cases from opposite sides of the immediate-action cutoff and distort which cases receive review. Consequently, the combined human--algorithm system can underperform the better of the human-only and algorithm-only benchmarks, even without any behavioral frictions. Full decision-maker liability eliminates the deployment-stage distortion.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Kenya's Cybersecurity Laws in Addressing the Cybersecurity Threats Posed by Social Media Apps
affiliations: Afronomicslaw

detail.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Kenya's Cybersecurity Laws in Addressing the Cybersecurity Threats Posed by Social Media Apps
detail.abstract: Social media is an essential part of modern society. It creates a community where people from diverse backgrounds, genders, countries and ages engage and interact at anytime from anywhere. Admittedly, social media offer many benefits. With one click of a button and a relatively strong internet connection, you can say hi to Xi in China while sitting comfortably in Kisumu. Additionally, social media has been very beneficial for businesses. Most businesses now use social media to market and advertise their products.  Users also use social media sites to get news updates with almost all government offices having social media handles.  Moreover, social media sites are used for entertainment with a large array of content creators posting content on social media. While social media sites have several advantages, they pose a threat to users. Social media sites offer a fertile ground for cybersecurity attacks. Sites like Facebook,  TikTok and WeChat have in the past been found liable for breaching cybersecurity and data privacy policies. This paper evaluates the threat posed by social media sites to cybersecurity in Kenya.

title: AI Exposure and Organizational Structure
affiliations: and Harvard University - Harvard Business School

detail.title: AI Exposure and Organizational Structure
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified debate about whether AI will flatten organizational hierarchies by substituting for managerial functions or instead expand them by generating new coordination and oversight demands. Despite strong claims from executives and consultants, evidence on how AI exposure reshapes core organizational structures remains limited. We address this gap by examining whether and how AI exposure affects two fundamental dimensions of organizational design: hierarchy depth and managerial span of control. We exploit staggered exposure to AI, defined as the presence of employees with AI-related skills, across 7,681 U.S. firms between 1990 and 2020 and implement a difference-indifferences research design. We find that AI exposure is associated with systematic restructuring of organizations. Firms exposed to AI reduce the number of hierarchical ranks while simultaneously increasing managerial spans of control, consistent with a flattening of organizational hierarchies. These effects are economically meaningful and heterogeneous: they are stronger in technical firms, in industries with higher automation intensity, and in organizations with greater technical expertise among managers and employees. Our findings contribute to the literature on organizational design and technology by moving beyond individual-level productivity effects to show how AI reshapes the internal structure of firms. For managers and policymakers, the results provide evidence-based guidance on how AI adoption interacts with hierarchy and managerial scope, thereby helping organizations redesign structures in ways that are both technologically enabled and organizationally sustainable.

title: Artificial Intelligence, System Optimization, and Corporate Strategy: Why AI Will Not Replace You-But Someone Who Knows How to Use It Will
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, System Optimization, and Corporate Strategy: Why AI Will Not Replace You-But Someone Who Knows How to Use It Will
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is often framed as a labor-replacement technology that threatens to displace human workers and automate entire professions. This paper argues that such framing is analytically incomplete. Artificial intelligence is better understood as infrastructure for applied optimization within modern organizations. Rather than eliminating human labor, AI accelerates the processes through which information is generated, analyzed, and integrated into decision-making systems.

Using concepts drawn from network optimization—including shortest path, minimal spanning tree, maximum flow, and sensitivity analysis—this paper develops a framework for understanding how AI reshapes organizational performance and labor market outcomes. The analysis argues that AI reduces informational path length, increases analytical throughput, and shifts the location of binding constraints within decision systems. As information becomes less scarce, judgment, governance, and strategic framing become the dominant constraints on organizational performance.

These dynamics produce a widening performance gap between actors who integrate AI into optimization processes and those who do not. At the firm level, AI functions as a structural capability amplifier: organizations that redesign workflows around augmented decision systems can accelerate sensing, learning, and strategic reconfiguration. At the individual level, the key differentiator becomes what this paper terms objective-function literacy—the ability to define decision goals, specify constraints, and supervise AI outputs within structured problem frameworks.

The paper further examines governance risks associated with poorly specified optimization objectives, particularly in areas such as AI-driven recruitment systems. Misaligned objective functions can amplify institutional bias and operational risk if constraints are not explicitly defined.

The central claim is that artificial intelligence will not replace competent professionals or well-managed firms. However, professionals and firms that understand how to use AI to optimize systems will outperform those that do not. The emerging competitive divide in modern business is therefore not technological access but optimization literacy.

detail.abstract:
The Cross-Layer Predictive Logistics Optimization Model (CPLOM) introduces a predictive control architecture for real-time multi-warehouse logistics networks operating under high demand volatility and interdependent system constraints.

Unlike traditional modular optimization approaches that isolate routing, warehouse operations, and workforce allocation, CPLOM formalizes logistics as a nonlinear dynamic system and implements a closed-loop adaptive control framework.

The architecture integrates multi-horizon forecasting, quantitative time-series analysis, neural decision modeling, and hybrid deterministic verification to constrain stochastic variability in mission-critical operations.

A novel contribution of this work is the interdisciplinary transfer of quantitative finance methodologies (e.g., volatility analysis, Bollinger Bands, momentum indicators) into physical logistics, transforming operational metrics into controllable dynamic indices.

Production deployment across multiple operational models demonstrates substantial throughput growth, reduced delivery time, improved resource efficiency, and architectural scalability.

CPLOM establishes a framework for predictive equilibrium in logistics systems, enabling autonomous adaptation to volatile demand, constrained resources, and external disruptions.

title: Platform Constitutionalism: The Digital Services Act and the Remaking of Internet Governance

detail.title: Platform Constitutionalism: The Digital Services Act and the Remaking of Internet Governance

publicationDetails.detailsText: in John Rothchild (ed), Research Handbook of Electronic Commerce Law (Edward Elgar, forthcoming 2026)

detail.abstract: The story of internet regulation begins with a paradox. The laws that helped create an open, innovative, and participatory digital environment also helped produce the concentrated private power that now governs much of public life online. The safe harbours of the 1990s and early 2000s were designed to protect intermediaries from becoming the enforcement deputies of states and rightholders. They succeeded. But in succeeding, they enabled the rise of platforms whose influence now extends far beyond mere intermediation: they rank, recommend, remove, amplify, and monetise speech at a scale that makes them de facto governors of the digital public sphere. This chapter argues that the Digital Services Act is Europe's attempt to respond to that transformation without destroying the legal architecture on which the internet economy was built. The DSA does not repudiate the e-Commerce Directive's liability settlement. It preserves the safe harbours and the prohibition on general monitoring. But it no longer leaves that settlement politically or constitutionally unstructured. Instead, it overlays immunity with due diligence duties, procedural rights, transparency requirements, systemic risk obligations, and an enforcement framework designed to subject the largest platforms to public accountability. In that sense, the DSA's deepest innovation is not simply regulatory intensity. It is constitutional ambition. Set against the continuing resilience of section 230 in the United States, the DSA reveals a widening transatlantic divergence between two models of internet governance: one centred on marketplace immunity and private editorial freedom, the other on democratic oversight, fundamental rights, and the disciplining of private power. Through an analysis of the DSA's layered obligations, VLOP regime, recommender-system rules, advertising restrictions, researcher access, crisis powers, and early enforcement practice, the chapter contends that the Act's broader significance lies in what it makes newly plausible: the idea that platform governance can be brought within the reach of democratic law.

title: How did Digitalization Affect Company Performance During the Covid-19 Pandemic? A Developing Economy Perspective
affiliations: University of Kragujevac - Faculty of Economics, Western Serbia Academy of Applied Studies and University of Kragujevac - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: How did Digitalization Affect Company Performance During the Covid-19 Pandemic? A Developing Economy Perspective
detail.abstract: The study aims to examine the impact of company digitalization on its response to the COVID-19 pandemic and financial performance. It also aims to examine the impact of company response to the COVID-19 pandemic on financial performance and the mediating role of company response to the COVID-19 pandemic in the relationship between company digitalization and financial performance. The results show that the more digitalized companies have responded to the COVID-19 pandemic more successfully and managed to improve their long-term financial performance. They also managed to improve their short-term financial performance but only indirectly, through response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The study contributes to the literature on the direct and indirect effects of digitalization on company financial performance in periods of crisis like the COVID-19 pandemic and the specificities of these effects in developing and transitioning economies. The study results have practical implications for company managers and owners, as well as policymakers in developing and transitioning economies similar to Serbian.

title: The Cost of Broken Promises: Does a Firm's Environmental Footprint Affect its Brand Equity?
affiliations: McGill University and Texas A&M University (TAMU), Central Texas

detail.title: The Cost of Broken Promises: Does a Firm's Environmental Footprint Affect its Brand Equity?
detail.abstract: Do customers punish a firm that harms the natural environment? We answer this question by examining the relationship between a firm's environmental footprint and customers' perceptions, as reflected in customer-based brand equity. Our empirical analysis shows that a firm's environmental footprint is negatively associated with its brand equity. Furthermore, the firm's advertising and CSR reputation aggravate this negative association. These results are consistent with the notion that customers view a large environmental footprint as a violation of the firm's brand promise. Follow-up analysis indicates that the association between a firm's environmental footprint and its brand equity is driven by resource use, rather than pollution, suggesting that customers interpret a firm's high resource use as a promissory violation. Additionally, the firm's environmental footprint is negatively associated with its brand stature but not its strength. The findings contribute to the environmental ethics literature and the brand-as-promise framework.

title: Economic Growth and Youth Unemployment in South Africa: A Dynamic Analysis of Structural Constraints and Policy Implications

detail.title: Economic Growth and Youth Unemployment in South Africa: A Dynamic Analysis of Structural Constraints and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: This paper examines the complex relationship between economic growth and youth unemployment in South Africa using annual time series data from 2000 to 2024. Despite experiencing periods of economic expansion, South Africa has maintained persistently high youth unemployment rates, with a mean of 53.036% during the study period, challenging conventional economic theories such as Okun's Law. The research employs a comprehensive methodological framework, including descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, distributed lag models, structural break tests, and robustness checks, to uncover the nuanced dynamics of this relationship. Key findings reveal a weak contemporaneous relationship between GDP growth and youth unemployment (Pearson r =-0.3468, R² = 0.1203), but significant lagged effects emerge when considering previous periods. A distributed lag model incorporating current and two lagged GDP growth terms explains 61.32% of youth unemployment variation, with a long-run multiplier of-2.2526, indicating that sustained 1% GDP growth leads to approximately 2.25% reduction in youth unemployment over time. Structural break analysis identifies 2019 as the most significant break point, suggesting that pre-COVID factors such as electricity crises and institutional decay have fundamentally altered the growth-unemployment nexus. The study demonstrates that while economic growth is necessary for youth job creation, it is insufficient alone to address South Africa's youth unemployment crisis. Policy scenario analysis projects that even optimistic 4% annual GDP growth would only reduce youth unemployment to 49.2% by 2034. The research concludes that comprehensive strategies combining growth-oriented policies with targeted interventions addressing structural constraints particularly energy sector reforms, education and skills development, labour market interventions, and spatial development strategies are essential for meaningful progress in reducing youth unemployment. These findings contribute to the literature on labour market dynamics in developing economies and provide evidence-based insights for policymakers seeking to address one of South Africa's most pressing socioeconomic challenges. The study highlights the need for a multidimensional approach that recognizes the unique structural characteristics of the South African labour market and the time-lagged nature of employment responses to economic growth.

title: Is an Algorithm Enough to Boost Purchase? The Interplay of the Viewer Targeting and Information Provision in Live-Streaming Commerce
affiliations: Tianjin University, Pennsylvania State University - Department of Supply Chain & Information Systems, Indiana University - Kelley School of Business and College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University

detail.title: Is an Algorithm Enough to Boost Purchase? The Interplay of the Viewer Targeting and Information Provision in Live-Streaming Commerce
detail.abstract: Algorithmic Viewer Targeting (AVT) is widely used in live-streaming commerce to direct high-potential consumers into ongoing sales sessions. Yet, in highly fluid viewing environments of livestreams, its effectiveness depends not only on targeting precision but also on how targeted viewers are engaged after arrival. This study investigates the conditions under which AVT leads to higher spending and the conversion of viewer-to-sales by examining its interaction with two key forms of in-session information provision: streamer expressions (informative vs. persuasive) and viewer comments (self-generated vs. other-generated). Using detailed consumer-journey data from influencer and store livestream sessions on a major live-streaming platform, we examine the purchase responses of AVT-targeted viewers and organically acquired viewers. We find that in store sessions, targeted viewers respond more strongly to informative expressions and less to persuasive expressions compared to organically acquired viewers, and such a pattern reverses in influencer sessions. Moreover, across influencer and store livestreams, targeted viewers' purchases are more strongly associated with their own commenting activity, whereas organically acquired viewers are more influenced by the volume of peer viewers' comments. These findings extend targeted advertising literature by shifting the focus from pre-acquisition targeting precision to postacquisition engagement alignment. They also provide operational guidance for livestream platforms and merchants: AVT investments deliver higher returns when real-time engagement strategies are tailored to both the viewer's origin and session format.

title: Pass-Through Of International Fossil Fuel Prices to Electricity Prices
affiliations: The University of Sydney - School of Economics, The University of Sydney and The University of Sydney

detail.title: Pass-Through Of International Fossil Fuel Prices to Electricity Prices
detail.abstract: We estimate pass-through of international fossil fuel prices to wholesale electricity prices in Australia, where approximately 85% of coal and 75% of natural gas is exported. Using station-level offer prices from the National Electricity Market over the period 2018-2023, we find strong pass-through. For black coal power stations, long-run pass-through of coal export prices is approximately 70%, though short-run variations remain insulated. For natural gas power stations, the relevant international benchmark shifts, depending on spare LNG export capacity. Before 2021, the Asian spot price (JKM) is passed through in full. Thereafter, it is passed through only when export terminals have spare capacity: during Australian winters. Otherwise, Brent is passed through, consistent with reported Brent-linked natural gas contract prices. Storage operators - both reservoir hydro and short-cycle storage - also pass through international fossil fuel prices, at rates comparable to thermal generators. This reflects the dependence of their opportunity costs on fossil fuels. These findings have direct policy implications. Our results suggest that a proposed gas reservation policy may not reduce electricity prices during peak winter periods, and that international commodity futures offer electricity market participants a practical tool for hedging wholesale price risk.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of political advertising on household consumption behavior in the United States. Using a regression discontinuity design that exploits variation in advertisement exposure across media market borders, we show that exposure to political advertisements significantly affects household consumption. Weekly county-level nondurable spending increases by 0.24% for every additional one standard deviation of positive economic-themed advertisements. The effect is heterogeneous by county-level demographics, with a stronger consumption response from counties with a higher proportion of older and low-income residents. We also provide evidence on the underlying mechanisms, showing that these effects operate through changes in household sentiment and the economic information conveyed in the advertisements.

title: Systemic Risk Radar: A Multi-Layer Graph Framework for Early Market Crash Prediction
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Systemic Risk Radar: A Multi-Layer Graph Framework for Early Market Crash Prediction
detail.abstract: Financial crises emerge when structural vulnerabilities accumulate across sectors, markets, and investor behavior. Predicting these systemic transitions is challenging because they arise from evolving interactions between market participants, not isolated price movements. We present Systemic Risk Radar (SRR), a framework that models financial markets as multi-layer graphs to detect early signs of systemic fragility and crash-regime transitions.  We evaluate SRR across three major crises: the Dot-com crash, the Global Financial Crisis, and the COVID-19 shock. Our experiments compare snapshot GNNs, a simplified temporal GNN prototype, and standard baselines (logistic regression and Random Forest). Results show that structural network information provides useful early-warning signals compared to feature-based models alone. This correlation-based instantiation of SRR shows that graph-derived features capture meaningful changes in market structure during stress events. The findings motivate extending SRR with additional graph layers (sector/factor exposure, sentiment) and advanced temporal architectures (LSTM/GRU or Transformer encoders) to better handle diverse crisis types.

title: Momentum Exhaustion and Fair Value Reversion: An ADX-conditioned VWAP Strategy in FX Markets

detail.title: Momentum Exhaustion and Fair Value Reversion: An ADX-conditioned VWAP Strategy in FX Markets
detail.abstract: This paper develops a regime-conditioned trading framework for foreign exchange markets that exploits intraday mean reversion toward a volume-weighted fair value benchmark under conditions of momentum exhaustion. Three dimensions are integrated: price location relative to previous-session extremes, deviation from the Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP), and trend strength as measured by Wilder's Average Directional Index (ADX). The strategy generates short (long) signals when price reaches prior-session highs (lows) while simultaneously exhibiting large positive (negative) VWAP deviations and a turning-over ADX, which collectively indicate that directional momentum is fading. The model bridges market-microstructure theory-specifically the role of VWAP as an institutional benchmark price-with technical regime filtering, contributing a theoretically grounded, state-conditioned mean-reversion framework to the FX literature. Formal backtesting and performance attribution are left to future work.

title: Extreme Connectedness among Energy Transition Metals and Commodity Markets

detail.title: Extreme Connectedness among Energy Transition Metals and Commodity Markets

detail.abstract: The global energy transition is reshaping commodity demand, yet its implications for commodity risk transmission remain unclear. We analyze connectedness among Energy Transition Metals (ETMs)-a subset of metals that are key inputs in clean energy technologies-energy commodities, and industrial metals using a Quantile Factor VAR framework. We document strong state dependence: spillovers are substantially larger in the tails of the return distribution than at the median. While crude oil remains influential, its dominance weakens post-Covid as ETMs, particularly base ETMs, gain centrality. A complementary event-study shows ETM-related policy announcements amplify spillovers in extreme regimes, indicating structural reconfiguration and systemic implications.

title: Algorithmic Gatekeeping
affiliations: INSEAD and Nanyang Technological University - Nanyang Business School

detail.title: Algorithmic Gatekeeping

publicationDetails.journalName: INSEAD Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: When should routing authority in tiered service systems transfer from human gatekeepers to algorithms? The answer hinges on an inseparable bundle. A human gatekeeper who interacts with customers can elicit contextual cues outside the algorithmic data pipeline, but the same unverifiability that makes these cues inaccessible to algorithms makes them impossible to fully contract on, exposing the system to agency distortion. Transferring authority to an algorithm eliminates both. The regime question is therefore whether to accept or reject this bundle. We formalize this tradeoff by decomposing customer complexity into hard information (observable by both humans and algorithms) and soft information (residual information that remain with frontline humans). We derive exact cost representations for each regime and a local frontier approximation: algorithmic routing dominates when |a| > c(v) √v, where a measures agency distortion, v measures soft information variance, and c(v) captures how the density of marginal cases differs between regimes. As soft information vanishes, the frontier simplifies to the distribution-free condition |a| > √v. We further show that increasing soft information variance can simultaneously raise algorithmic errors and reduce agency costs, a finding that helps explain why human gatekeeping persists in high-uncertainty environments. Hybrid pre-screening exhibits a sharp asymmetry: it mitigates under-referral but not over-referral, reflecting structural limits of partial unbundling. Extensions to heterogeneous gatekeepers, imperfect information processing, signaldependent variance, and human-contact costs show the frontier generalizes with modified parameters. Our analysis reframes routing technology adoption from "how accurate is the algorithm?" to "who should hold routing authority?"

detail.abstract: Rapid urbanization combined with increasing climate variability has significantly intensified urban flood risk, particularly in rapidly growing cities with limited planning capacity (Wu et al., 2024). Urban flood susceptibility assessment has therefore become a critical tool for supporting sustainable land-use planning and disaster risk reduction strategies (Cai et al., 2024). This study applied a GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis framework integrating the Analytic Hierarchy Process and weighted overlay techniques to model urban flood susceptibility (Nguyen et al., 2024). Multiple spatial data layers, including topography, land use and land cover, drainage density, rainfall intensity, and proximity to water bodies, were standardized and integrated within a GIS environment (Wu et al., 2024). Criterion weights were derived using pairwise comparisons to reflect the relative influence of physical and anthropogenic factors on flood occurrence (Cai et al., 2024). The resulting flood susceptibility map revealed distinct spatial patterns, with high-risk zones concentrated in low-lying areas characterized by dense drainage networks and extensive impervious surfaces (Nguyen et al., 2024). Land-use change and inadequate drainage infrastructure emerged as dominant contributors to elevated flood susceptibility (Wu et al., 2024). Overall, the findings demonstrate that GIS-based MCDA provides a transparent, systematic, and decision-oriented framework for urban flood risk assessment and planning (Cai et al., 2024).

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Nash & Cibinic Report, Volume 36, Issue 4, April 2022

detail.abstract:
Recent developments in bid protest corrective actions and voluntary remands at the Court of Federal Claims (COFC) and Government Accountability Office (GAO).

When a protester succeeds in establishing prejudicial error, the result is almost always that the agency is directed back to the drawing board to decide its next move. Neither the Government Accountability Office nor the U.S. Court of Federal Claims will usurp the agency's procurement function by dictating in the first instance how an agency should write its solicitation or which company should receive a contract award. This feeds a common critique that protests can be futile, because even if a protester identifies an error, the agency can often find a way to document a rationale for selecting the same awardee or issuing the same solicitation.
Nevertheless, protests can and often do achieve important objectives, including shaping critical solicitation terms, eliminating barriers to competition (even eliminating competitors), bringing important information to light, restructuring or abandonment of an acquisition strategy, and in some cases changing the award decision in the protester's favor. It is critical for contractors and their counsel to carefully think through the business case for filing any given protest; the analysis cannot be limited to the likelihood of prevailing in litigation but must also consider the probable outcome once the agency is back at the drawing board.

Of course, agencies are not required to wait until the GAO or the COFC issues a final decision to take matters back into their own hands. Agencies have significant leeway to take corrective action in response to a protest and, instead of investing time and resources in defending litigation, revisit their procurement decisions in light of the protest arguments. Although not formally defined, the term corrective action “in the bid protest context generally means agency action, usually taken after a protest has been initiated, to correct a perceived prior error in the procurement process, or, in the absence of error, to act to improve the competitive process.” Dellow Corp. v. United States, 855 F.3d 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2017), 59 GC ¶ 143.

Because an agency's decision to take corrective action often amounts to the same relief that the protester could win on the merits, there is an initial inclination by the protester to celebrate, followed by the sobering realization that the agency may be taking corrective action only to bolster its administrative record and reinforce the same decision that the protester challenged. This can be one of the most critical junctions of a bid protest, yet it is governed by an under-developed, unpublished, and internally inconsistent body of procedural norms and precedent. It is imperative for protest counsel to understand the rules and standards that apply to corrective action and remand activities at the GAO and the court. This area of procurement has been quite active over the past few years in both forums, with more developments likely.

title: Rivalrous Remedies
affiliations: Stigler Center, University of Chicago Booth School of Business and Tel Aviv University - Buchmann Faculty of Law

detail.title: Rivalrous Remedies
detail.abstract:
Legal scholarship typically conceptualizes enforcement as operating directly on wrongdoers: either by enjoining them ex ante or by imposing monetary sanctions on them ex post. Yet across a wide range of legal fields, courts and lawmakers have long employed a different and largely untheorized instrument. Instead of sanctioning the wrongdoer directly, these doctrines deter misconduct by conferring a legal advantage on the wrongdoer’s rival: a business competitor, a litigation counterparty, or another strategically positioned actor. For example, when a patent holder forces customers to sign aggressive licensing agreements, courts may allow the patent holder’s competitors to freely infringe the patent. And in family law, when one parent alienates a child from the other, courts often respond not by fining the alienator parent but by granting the alienated parent additional visitation rights.

This Article is the first to systematically analyze this institutional design, which we term “rivalrous remedies.” In the process, the Article makes three contributions. Conceptually, it identifies the conditions under which regulating behavior indirectly—by empowering rivals—can outperform classic remedies. Rivalrous remedies can leverage the superior information and incentives of rivals. At the same time, these remedies operate effectively only in certain market structures and pose risks of overuse and spillover harms to third parties.

Descriptively, the Article demonstrates the prevalence of rivalrous remedies by analyzing nine doctrines across diverse legal fields: from false advertising to defamation law to civil procedure. While each doctrine has been criticized by scholars in their respective fields, viewing them through a common lens reveals a shared institutional logic: they emerged to address chronic underenforcement problems. In particular, these doctrines respond to underenforcement by shifting who enforces (not necessarily the direct victim) and/or how enforcement occurs (through largely self-executed mechanisms requiring minimal judicial involvement).

Normatively, the Article offers guidance for courts interpreting existing rivalrous remedies, identifying when they should be expanded, constrained, or combined with traditional remedies. It also proposes the adoption of a new rivalrous remedy in trade secret law to address enforcement failures surrounding consumers’ “right to repair.”

title: Online Traffic Games: Should Firms Compete on Website Speed or Website Capacity?
affiliations: C. T. Bauer College of Business, University of Houston and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Online Traffic Games: Should Firms Compete on Website Speed or Website Capacity?
detail.abstract: In today's fast-paced digital world, consumers demand instant access to online content and are intolerant of delays, making website speed a key competitive advantage in attracting web traffic. Google's Speed Update and Core Web Vitals have further emphasized the significance of website speed in web traffic competition. This study examines how firms strategically compete for web traffic by managing website speed, focusing specifically on two distinct strategies: response-based and capacity-based. Under response-based competition, firms first set their desired website speed (or equivalently, website response time), subsequently determining the necessary website capacity. In contrast, in capacity-based competition, firms initially select the website capacity level, which in turn determines the website response time. We analyze a duopoly scenario in which two firms compete for web traffic. Although website speed and capacity are functionally related, surprisingly, firms sometimes compete more aggressively under responsebased competition. Interestingly, the aggression of response-based competition can sometimes increase firms' profits. We also show that when firms freely choose the decision process, firms sometimes engage in a mode of competition in equilibrium, which yields a lower profit for the capacity provider (e.g., computing capacity provider) than the alternative mode. We further show how the cloud provider can increase profit by strategically inducing firms to engage in a preferred mode of competition. This is achieved by lowering the unit price of renting capacity related to that mode of competition. This strategic price reduction can lead to faster websites for consumers, an increase in the provider's revenue, and consequently an increase in the cloud provider's profit under a cost-efficiency condition. The profit of firms can sometimes increase too, implying a win-win-win for all the parties, namely, firms, consumers, and the provider.

detail.abstract: This study examines how Geographic Information Systems (GIS) can be used to monitor land use change and evaluate planning compliance in rapidly urbanizing regions. detail.abstract: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act) represents a transformative shift in India's secured credit enforcement regime. Enacted in response to mounting non-performing assets and systemic inefficiencies in debt recovery, the Act introduced a non-judicial enforcement mechanism empowering secured creditors to realise collateral without prior court adjudication. This research undertakes a comprehensive doctrinal, constitutional, institutional, and socioeconomic analysis of the SARFAESI framework. The study examines the conceptual foundations of securitisation and asset reconstruction, the legislative architecture of enforcement under Section 13, and the jurisdictional structure encompassing District Magistrates, Debts Recovery Tribunals (DRTs), Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunals (DRATs), and constitutional courts. Particular attention is devoted to the constitutional validity of the Act, especially in light of Article 300A (right to property), principles of natural justice, and judicial interpretation in landmark decisions such as Mardia Chemicals, Transcore, and subsequent jurisprudence. The research further evaluates the interaction between SARFAESI and other recovery mechanisms, including the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, highlighting jurisdictional overlaps and priority doctrines. Through empirical analysis of NPA trends and recovery data, the paper assesses the statute's effectiveness in improving credit discipline while critically engaging with concerns regarding proportionality, borrower vulnerability, tribunal capacity, and institutional delay. Comparative insights from the United States and United Kingdom secured transactions frameworks are incorporated to situate SARFAESI within global best practices. The study concludes that while SARFAESI has significantly strengthened secured credit enforcement and contributed to financial stability, its long-term legitimacy depends upon robust tribunal infrastructure, procedural transparency, and harmonised coordination with insolvency law. The Act emerges as a calibrated instrument of economic governance-efficient yet constitutionally conditioned.

detail.title: Stakeholder Populism, Campaign GM, and the Economic Education of the Public
detail.abstract: Populism does not sit well with corporate social responsibility because it tends to collapse all stakeholders into one group, "the people." We consider an alternative relationship between populism and corporate social responsibility, which we capture in the notion of stakeholder populism. We show how, in a historically contingent time and place-the late 1960s and early 1970s in the United States-a group of activist lawyers known as the Project on Corporate Responsibility posited themselves as representatives of "the people," understood as the numerous stakeholders of the American corporation, and campaigned to impose socially responsible behavior on the management of General Motors (GM) and subsequently other large US corporations. Setting the Project against the broader mutations of postwar liberalism, we draw on new archival material to trace the making of Campaign GM and consider how this turning point in the history of corporate governance was also catalyst for the regrouping of the business establishment and the strategic reorientation of its efforts toward the economic education of the public.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of organizational culture on employee performance in the aviation sector, with a specific focus on Pakistan International Airlines (PIA). Drawing upon Job Characteristics Theory (JCT) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the research investigates how cultural values, leadership practices, and communication patterns influence both task and contextual performance. Furthermore, the study introduces aviation-specific occupational identity as a moderating variable, proposing that employees who strongly identify with their professional aviation roles respond differently to cultural influences. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, data were collected from 412 employees across operational, technical, and administrative departments. Multiple regression and moderation analyses reveal that organizational culture has a significant positive effect on employee performance, and this relationship is strengthened when aviation-specific occupational identity is high. The findings contribute to organizational behavior and aviation HRM literature by integrating identity-based motivation within a culture–performance framework. Practically, the study offers strategic insights for improving employee engagement, motivation, and performance in state-owned and safety-critical organizations.

title: Measuring Supply Chain Resilience: A Perspective Inspired by Material Mechanics
affiliations: , Fudan University - School of Management and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: Measuring Supply Chain Resilience: A Perspective Inspired by Material Mechanics
detail.abstract: Global disruptions, ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic to trade conflicts, have elevated supply chain resilience (SCR) to a priority for governments worldwide. Yet the lack of a practical measurement framework, particularly at the industry level, limits efforts to move resilience from an abstract notion to a quantity that can be analyzed and optimized. Measuring industry-level SCR presents substantial methodological challenges. In particular, meaningful metrics should satisfy three requirements: they should adopt a network perspective while remaining computationally tractable; they should be intrinsic properties of the supply chain network (SCN), independent of assumed disruption scenarios or probability spaces; and they should reflect the adaptability of the SCN. Drawing inspiration from measures of material resilience, we propose two resilience metrics for SCNs that satisfy all three requirements. We formulate a linear programming model to compute the proposed metrics and demonstrate their practical relevance through three case studies. The results provide a unified framework for industry-level resilience analysis and offer insights relevant for macrolevel supply chain governance.

detail.abstract: Career incentives distort bureaucratic behavior, but do these distortions persist over time? We exploit a discontinuity in promotion incentives at age 58 among Chinese prefecture-level party secretaries during the enforcement of the zero-Covid policy (2021–2022). Officials with stronger promotion incentives increase enforcement probability by 0.73 percentage points per unit rise in cases—approximately a 10 percent increase relative to the baseline—operating across spatial, temporal, and administrative dimensions. The distortion attenuates with accumulated outbreak management experience: each additional 100 days of experience reduces promotion-driven enforcement by roughly one quarter of its initial magnitude, following a smooth learning pattern consistent with experience-based updating. Importantly, heightened enforcement does not prolong outbreak duration. Instead, welfare costs are front-loaded during officials’ initial crisis responses and are concentrated in sector-specific disruptions.

detail.abstract: This article examines how long-term orientation (LTO) as a cultural dimension influences consumer brand loyalty, addressing contradictory directions in existing research. Building on theoretical insights from cross-cultural research, with evidence from four studies using primary and secondary data across diverse samples consistently showing that high-LTO consumers exhibit lower brand loyalty. This negative effect is driven by the self-flexibility facet of LTO culture-an individuals' tendency to adapt the self to changing circumstances. Both across and within cultures, high-LTO individuals exhibit greater self-flexibility, which weakens their tendency to form strong relationship with a brand (i.e., self-brand connection), which in turn, reduces their brand loyalty. This negative effect of LTO is particularly more pronounced for exchange-oriented and low-involvement brands, for which self-brand connection is highly malleable and culturally influenced. These findings contribute to the cross-culture, loyalty and consumer-brand relationship literatures by clarifying the role of LTO culture in shaping consumer-brand relationships, offering actionable insights for managers, and opening new avenues for future research.

title: Augmentation or Atrophy? A Critical Analysis of Gen Z's Use of Generative AI in Learning Contexts
affiliations: Mindanao State University - Iligan Institute of Technology

detail.title: Augmentation or Atrophy? A Critical Analysis of Gen Z's Use of Generative AI in Learning Contexts
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) among Gen Z has intensified concerns about its dual role as both a productivity enhancer and a potential source of cognitive decline. Drawing on a recent large-scale survey of young adults, this article critically examines claims that AI use undermines critical thinking, learning-bydoing, and social interaction. Using Cognitive Load Theory and the Substitution-Augmentation framework as analytical lenses, the paper argues that these concerns are conceptually overstated and insufficiently theorized. Rather than inherently diminishing cognitive capability, generative AI redistributes cognitive effort, reducing extraneous load while potentially enhancing germane processing when used appropriately. The analysis further demonstrates that negative outcomes are primarily associated with substitutional use of AI, whereas augmentative use can support deeper learning and skill development. However, the underlying evidence base remains largely descriptive and perception-driven, limiting causal inference. The article concludes that the central challenge for educators is not regulating AI usage per se, but designing learning environments that promote augmentation and constrain substitution. By reframing AI adoption as an instructional design problem rather than a behavioral control issue, this study offers a more precise foundation for integrating generative AI into educational practice.

title: Which Review Signals Drive Sales of High-Involvement Durable Goods? Evidence from Toyota RAV4 in the U.S

detail.title: Which Review Signals Drive Sales of High-Involvement Durable Goods? Evidence from Toyota RAV4 in the U.S
detail.abstract: Online reviews are an important information source in high-involvement durable-goods markets, yet their incremental explanatory power at the individual vehicle-model level remains unclear. Focusing on the Toyota RAV4, the best-selling car in the U.S. in 2025, this study constructs a 19-year monthly dataset combining vehicle sales, online reviews, Google Trends, macroeconomic indicators, and major market shocks. Grounded in the Heuristic-Systematic Model (HSM), the study compares multiple review signals using monthly time-series regressions that account for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation. The results show that, once macroeconomic conditions, search volume, and calendar effects are rigorously controlled, online review signals provide limited additional explanatory power. Among the measures examined, a sentiment signal based on a simple aggregation of the latest 25 reviews shows the most stable positive association with next-month sales in the preferred specification. By contrast, adding recency or helpfulness weights does not consistently improve model performance. Vehicle recommendation rate and several attribute-level rating measures occasionally yield comparable model fit, but their coefficients are not robust across specifications. Overall, the findings suggest that, in high-involvement durable-goods markets, online reviews function as supplementary rather than dominant indicators of demand. More broadly, the study contributes to the online review literature by introducing a behaviorally grounded measurement approach that better reflects the limited set of recently visible reviews consumers are likely to process before purchase.

title: Capability Inflation in AI-Integrated Education: A Framework for Human Capital Preservation Under Accelerating Automation

detail.title: Capability Inflation in AI-Integrated Education: A Framework for Human Capital Preservation Under Accelerating Automation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial, institutional, or personal conflicts of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and received no financial support from public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agencies.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming higher education systems worldwide, reshaping teaching, learning, assessment, and graduate preparation. While AI adoption promises efficiency and innovation, unstructured integration may generate a structural risk: potential divergence between observable academic performance and independently verifiable human capability. This paper defines that divergence as Capability Inflation—a condition in which the period change in AI-augmented observable performance (ΔP) exceeds the period change in independently verifiable human capability (ΔICI), such that P = H + A but ΔP > ΔICI (see Section 3.4 for full operationalization; continuous-rate equivalent: dA/dt > dH/dt).

The risk is conditional, not inevitable. Its probability and magnitude depend on institutional design. A second, underappreciated dimension compounds it: AI mediation now operates at two layers simultaneously—the production layer (student outputs) and the verification layer (assessment design, feedback, grading). When both are AI-mediated without compensatory verification architecture, the institutional mechanisms that stabilise credential signals weaken from both ends. This dual-augmentation dynamic is underaddressed in most AI-in-education governance discourse.

In labour markets increasingly mediated by AI systems, graduates compete not only with peers but with automation capable of performing structured cognitive tasks at low marginal cost. Human competitive advantage depends on maintaining capability growth above the rising complementarity threshold. Educational systems that permit cognitive substitution during formative years risk weakening employability, compressing early-career opportunity, and undermining long-term economic resilience.

This paper proposes the Graduate Capability Protection Standard (GCPS) , a phased institutional framework—spanning transparency, capability verification, and structural embedding—designed to align AI integration with human capital preservation. The framework is grounded in two co-equal rationales: the economic case for maintaining human complementarity above the rising automation threshold, and the prior normative commitment that the capacity to reason and judge independently is a constitutive feature of educated persons and a precondition for epistemic autonomy in AI-mediated institutions. The framework introduces capability integrity principles, dual-mode assessment architecture, transparency requirements, educator safeguards, and monitoring mechanisms anchored in two complementary indices: the Independent Capability Index (ICI) and the Capability Inflation Index (CII).

The framework is explicitly falsifiable. If sustained multi-cohort evidence demonstrates that independent capability growth matches or exceeds observable performance growth, GCPS monitoring confirms alignment and triggers no corrective intervention. If divergence is detected, graduated intervention responds proportionally—and early detection reduces long-run recalibration costs, which rise significantly once substitution norms become institutionally embedded. The objective is not to restrict technological adoption, but to ensure that AI integration strengthens independent cognition, preserves credential signalling reliability, and sustains competitiveness under accelerating automation.

title: Public Relations Practices of the Presidency of Religious Affairs (Diyanet) in Friday Sermons (Khutbahs)

detail.title: Public Relations Practices of the Presidency of Religious Affairs (Diyanet) in Friday Sermons (Khutbahs)
detail.abstract: Public relations encompasses strategic communication activities through which institutions engage with their publics and establish legitimacy. While traditionally associated with corporate environments, public relations holds equal importance in public governance, where institutions disseminate social norms, policy priorities, and collective responsibilities to diverse audiences. In this broader context, state-affiliated religious institutions may also serve as significant communicative agents; however, their role within public relations scholarship remains insufficiently explored. This study analyzes Friday sermons (khutbahs) delivered nationwide in Türkiye by the Presidency of Religious Affairs (Diyanet) from 2020 to 2024 as an institutionalized public relations tool. Using qualitative content analysis of 269 sermons, including 115 sermons addressing diverse topics such as social solidarity, public health, disaster response, national unity, and global justice, the study examines how religious discourse addresses societal issues beyond theological teachings. The findings suggest that sermons serve as central communicative texts that reinforce civic responsibility, manage collective emotions during crises, and align moral stories with wider governance frameworks. The study introduces the idea of religion-based public-sector public relations, presenting a model where symbolic authority, ritual continuity, and value-driven persuasion act as mechanisms of soft governance. By integrating religious discourse into modern public relations theory, the article broadens the field's analytical scope and emphasizes the communicative power of culturally rooted public institutions.

title: Optimal Market-Making with Hawkes Process: A Markovian Approximation Approach via Mercer's Expansion

detail.title: Optimal Market-Making with Hawkes Process: A Markovian Approximation Approach via Mercer's Expansion
detail.abstract: We study an optimal market-making problem under which the order flow and liquidity level are driven by self-exciting Hawkes processes. To overcome the challenge brought by the non-Markovian structure of the problem, we propose a Markovian lifting approach where the Hawkes kernels are approximated by their truncated Mercer's expansions. This enables dynamic programming and in turn computationally feasible procedures to solve the market-making problem. The theoretical convergence of the approximated solution to the true value function is proven. Our numerical findings show that ignoring persistence with the order flow and liquidity level underestimates adverse selection risk, whereas explicitly modelling them improves the robustness and profitability of the market-making strategies.

title: The Speed-to-scrutiny Pradox in Social Media-driven HRM: Evidence from Albania

detail.title: The Speed-to-scrutiny Pradox in Social Media-driven HRM: Evidence from Albania
detail.abstract: Purpose: This study examines the dual role of social media in human resource management (HRM), highlighting how digital platforms simultaneously enhance recruitment efficiency while intensifying ethical, legal, and governance challenges. Focusing on Albania as a transition economy, the study explores how HR professionals navigate the tension between speed, reach, and visibility, and the requirements of fairness, privacy, and regulatory compliance. Design/methodology/approach: Drawing on McFarland and Ployhart's (2015) Discrete Ambient Stimuli (DAS) framework, the study adopts a qualitative multi-case design based on twelve semi-structured interviews with HR professionals across banking, technology, consulting, microfinance, and public administration. Data were analysed thematically, combining theorydriven coding with inductive insights from the Albanian context. Findings: The findings show that social media transform recruitment by enhancing accessibility, immediacy, and targeting precision, enabling faster and more cost-effective talent acquisition. However, these efficiencies are accompanied by heightened exposure to privacy risks, data permanence, and evaluative bias. The study identifies a "speed-to-scrutiny" paradox, whereby the same platform characteristics that accelerate recruitment also expand the scope of candidate evaluation and ethical vulnerability. In response, HR professionals develop emergent governance practices, including GDPR-aligned policies, "minimum data" principles, and ethical training, although implementation remains uneven across organisations. Originality/value: This study extends the DAS framework to a post-socialist context, demonstrating how platform-specific stimuli operate under conditions of institutional fluidity, SME dominance, and uneven regulatory enforcement. It advances the concept of the speed-toscrutiny paradox as a core mechanism linking digital efficiency with ethical complexity in HRM, and offers context-sensitive insights into how organisations develop hybrid governance practices in emerging digital labour markets.

title: Designing Positive Reality Framing the Frame
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Designing Positive Reality Framing the Frame
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a framework for modeling socioeconomic systems as evolutionary search processes navigating a four-dimensional state space-values and norms, properties and categories, change and competition, and knowledge and goods-rather than optimizing equilibrium. We formalize systemic coherence as Σ(R) = R ⊤ GR, where G captures inter-dimensional coupling, and define the viable frontier as the boundary between structured order and the reservoir of experimental possibilities. From this framework we derive three design principles: structural prevention of destructive dynamics, bounded positive feedback, and signal-coherent finance. We operationalize the framework using twenty-eight genuinely monthly macroeconomic seriesincluding political trust, ecosystem health, innovation output, and competitive dynamics indicators constructed entirely from free public sources-for 2005-2024 (N = 184). After Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, 32.4% of pairwise Granger links survive (six times the null rate), and all twelve inter-dimensional block exogeneity tests are significant at p < 0.0001. The systemic coherence index Σ(R) significantly predicts stress episodes at the six-month horizon (p < 0.0001), and low coherence amplifies VIX shock transmission into the abstract-layer dimensions (p < 0.001). A multi-event study across four crisis episodes (GFC, COVID-19, China Shock, Euro Crisis) reveals a dose-response gradient: direct-hit crises produce deep Σ collapse with asymmetric cross-dimensional transmission, while peripheral events show stable or rising coherence. Crosscountry replication for the US, Euro Area, and Japan confirms inter-dimensional coupling as a general macroeconomic feature. We interpret these results as evidence of recoverable predictive structure, not structural causation. A dimension-level VAR on four principal components extracted from 17 variables yields 58.3% Granger coupling density and confirms the temporal-scale asymmetry, and a two-stage least squares identification using the Kilian Index of Global Real Economic Activity provides directional causal evidence for the r 2 → r 3 coupling pathway (β = 0.52, p = 0.007, near-weak instrument; confirmed under Anderson-Rubin weak-instrument-robust inference, 95% CI excluding zero). Computational validation across 35,076 simulation runs-including an allocation-consequence extension that produced the first detectable propagation signal (p = 0.015) and the first significant counter-regulation recovery effect (p = 0.047)-a dimension-differentiated fourdimensional extension (1,900 additional runs) confirming dimension-specific vulnerability and propagation asymmetry, structured comparison of nine historical boundarydistortion episodes, and a crosscountry panel analysis (N = 80 countries, 2002-2022) 1 provide convergent evidence for the architecture's core predictions across three independent evidence layers. The panel confirms that counter-regulation significantly moderates crisis-induced coherence divergence (p = 0.004).

The study concludes that effective regulation requires enhanced transparency mechanisms, improved valuation standards, and stronger international cooperation. These measures are necessary to ensure equitable taxation in the digital era and to protect national revenue systems.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a general equilibrium model of a blockchain economy that comprises three markets: the market for block space; the market for security and consensus in a proof of work (PoW) regime; and, the market for cryptocurrency exchange. We first construct partial equilibrium models for each market before bringing them together in a general equilibrium framework. Comparative static exercises characterize how the fee rate paid by users, the network hash power and cryptocurrency prices respond to various shocks, including those that occur in the real economy, such as interest rate changes. We also assess how these shocks affect the security of the blockchain against a majority attack. The focus of the paper is on building a simple set of graphical tools that can be used to visualize how a blockchain economy operates.

title: Directed Improvisation with AI: A Syllabus

detail.title: Directed Improvisation with AI: A Syllabus
detail.abstract: This PhD seminar addresses a central challenge posed by generative AI across organizations: What becomes of human agency when AI can generate answers on demand—and what does it then mean to think and learn? In higher education, this appears as “students cheating with AI,” prompting bans or restrictions. This course takes a different approach. In a world where AI will be ubiquitous, the task is not to eliminate AI, but to redefine human agency—from producing answers to directing how humans and AI produce them together. Anchored in Yuen Yuen Ang’s idea of Directed Improvisation, the course develops this meta-skill of direction, treating AI not as a passive tool but as a complex, co-creative system whose outputs depend on how humans guide it. Moving beyond simple commands and prompts, and using experiments with bespoke knowledge infrastructure, students learn to shape AI’s paradigm—its underlying assumptions and concepts—diagnose its reasoning, and refine both AI outputs and their own thinking.

detail.abstract: Human decision-making has traditionally been explained through rational evaluation of benefits and consequences; however, real-world behavior frequently deviates from purely rational models. The Mesa 2:1 Theory proposes that all deliberate human thoughts and decisions arise from cognitive processes governed by psychological regulation, wherein individuals select options that create, enhance, maintain, or restore psychological equilibrium (homeostasis) and/or reduce internal psychological discomfort. The theory introduces the 2:1 Principle, wherein multiple possibilities are cognitively reduced into dominant competing alternatives, followed by a single final determination. This represents a cognitive bottleneck rather than a strict numerical rule. While the 2:1 structure explains the narrowing process, the theory emphasizes that the decisive element is the final determination (“1”), wherein one option attains regulatory dominance and produces action and its consequences. Decision-making operates across a continuum ranging from voluntary (internally dominant) conditions to coercive (externally constrained) conditions, with a corresponding shift toward survival-prioritized regulation under constraint. 2 Further, the theory establishes that decision outcomes are not fixed but are modifiable through systematic evaluation and alteration of the situational and psychological factors influencing regulatory dominance. This extends the model from a descriptive framework to an application-oriented approach, with relevance across psychology, criminology, education, mental health, and social behavior. The Mesa 2:1 Theory thus provides a unified, context-sensitive model of human decision-making that integrates cognitive structure, psychological regulation, contextual variability, and outcome modifiability, while offering a structured basis for understanding and influencing human behavior.

detail.title: AutoInventory: An Autonomous Research and Optimization Framework for Stochastic Inventory Problems
detail.abstract: We present AutoInventory, an autonomous framework that approaches the censored newsvendor problem through self-directed experimentation rather than analytical derivation. A human writes a business brief and a deterministic simulation harness; an agent edits a single policy file in a keep/discard loop. Applied to a simulated five-product perishable retail problem with censored demand, seasonal spikes, and substitution effects, the framework advances profit from 72.5% to 90.7% of the oracle bound across 645 experiments, 469 of which were discarded. The key findings are empirical: product-specific censoring corrections outperform uniform inflation, historical data weight is negative for stable-demand products, and post-holiday demand correction is as valuable as pre-holiday anticipation. The framework recovers approximately $99,000 in annual profit that a static policy leaves unrealized. The framework implements an autonomous research pattern: the human specifies the intent; the agent searches the policy space.

detail.title: Computing Non-Stationary (s, S) Policies: A Monte Carlo Approach and Benchmark Study
detail.abstract: We revisit the finite-horizon stochastic dynamic inventory problem with non-stationary demand, linear variable, holding and backlog costs, and a fixed ordering cost, for which the optimal policy is of the (s,S) type. While the policy structure is well-understood, computing the corresponding parameters is challenging, especially when demand distributions are non-standard or unknown. We propose a Monte Carlo dynamic programming approach that computes near-optimal non-stationary (s,S) policies directly from demand samples. The method builds on an existing data-driven recursion and combines it with grid-based interpolation and local refinement steps, which yields a simple and distribution-agnostic algorithm with a transparent trade-off between runtime and accuracy. We complement the method with a large-scale computational study that investigates parameter sensitivity and benchmarks our algorithm against two state-of-the-art approaches across multiple demand patterns, cost settings, and planning horizons. The results show that the proposed approach consistently achieves the smallest optimality gaps while remaining computationally efficient. Its performance advantage becomes more pronounced for longer planning horizons. Overall, the proposed method offers an attractive combination of accuracy, scalability, and practical applicability for computing non-stationary (s,S) policies.

detail.abstract: Driven by changing workforce expectations, digital transformation and AI, and environmental uncertainty, New Ways of Working (NWW) are reshaping organizations. Yet these empowered practices often collide with management control systems rooted in command-and-control orthodoxy, creating 'frustrated transformations'. This chapter examines these tensions by identifying misalignments between NWW-oriented leadership principles and legacy control routines. Drawing on the Viable Map, it starts from the premise that every organization operates with a management model-a configuration of leadership principles and management processes-and shows how their alignment shapes empowerment and adaptability, and thus performance.
