In doing so, it provides a structured way for managers and researchers to diagnose and design management controls suited to specific organizational contexts, enabling more empowering and adaptive management models in which autonomy and accountability reinforce each other.

detail.abstract: The past year reminds us of the rock lyrics from “Spinning Wheel” on Blood, Sweat & Tears’s 1968 self-titled record—“What goes up, must come down/Spinning Wheel got to go round”—because there have been many changes in strategy and reversal of policy since President Trump’s inauguration in January 2025. Our Survey documents these changes and reversals as they affect electronic payments and financial services. This year’s Survey also reports on warnings from state and federal regulators aimed at bank and non-bank providers of consumer financial services. Part II examines an FTC enforcement action related to the unfair and deceptive marketing of so-called “free” products. In Part III, we address a CFPB action against a peer-to-peer payments platform for failing to protect consumers from fraud. Part IV examines several federal enforcement actions that emphasize safety and soundness, as well as robust anti-money laundering programs. We also examine several cases that demonstrate how states are stepping up to address regulatory issues that are not being pursued at the federal level in Part V. In a similar vein, Part VI discusses developments in New York regarding Buy Now, Pay Later (“BNPL”) legislation in the wake of CFPB abandoning its regulatory authority over those products. In Part VII, we give a brief account of the federal government’s effort to impose economic sanctions on a “crypto mixer,” Tornado Cash, our only nod to our longstanding coverage of crypto currencies. We conclude in Part VIII with brief comments on—to borrow from the same refrain—what happens if you miss the “directing sign on the straight and narrow highway.” While the “spinning wheel” of regulatory pronouncements and retractions may prove dizzying to many observers, we trust this year’s Survey will help business lawyers provide a steadying hand and calming influence to nervous clients.

detail.abstract: We study how financially distressed firms adjust disclosure when creditor bargaining power increases. Exploiting the 2014 Marblegate Asset Management v. Education Management Corporation ruling, which unexpectedly strengthened public bondholders' ability to hold out in out-of-court restructurings, we find that distressed firms with publicly traded debt significantly reduce voluntary disclosure following the ruling. The decline is concentrated among firms with high blockholder ownership, consistent with informed shareholders curtailing public information to limit bondholders' ability to assess continuation values and coordinate holdout strategies. Disclosure reductions persist among firms with stable capital structures, ruling out financing switching as an alternative explanation. Remaining disclosures become more complex and litigious and are associated with lower likelihoods of positive market reactions. These changes coincide with a deterioration in market information environments and more restrictive covenants in subsequent bond issues. Our findings establish disclosure as a strategic instrument in debt renegotiation, with implications for financial reporting, creditor protection, and restructuring regulation.

detail.title: Monetizing Scarce Attention in Online Marketplaces: Decentralized Pricing, Assortment, and Endogenous Selling Fees
detail.abstract: Online marketplaces monetize seller access to demand through complex fee structures while managing strictly limited high-visibility capacity. We study how a retail platform should jointly choose a capacityconstrained featured assortment and per-unit selling fees when featured sellers compete on the platform. We formulate a Stackelberg game in which the platform selects the featured set and selling fees, and sellers then compete either in prices (Bertrand) or in market shares (Cournot) under multinomial logit demand. We characterize the platform's optimal curation and fee policies and establish simple structural results. Our analysis shows that a decentralized platform should always fully utilize its display capacity, ranking sellers by an "adjusted-cost attractiveness" metric that balances demand potential with cost efficiency. Importantly, we demonstrate that Bertrand competition consistently generates higher platform revenue and market share than Cournot competition, driven by platform leadership in controlling product exposure and fee structures and the resulting intensified price competition among sellers. Finally, we study a cooperative pricing benchmark in which the platform coordinates retail prices while guaranteeing sellers target profit levels. This problem is NP-hard and may optimally leave display capacity unused when seller participation rents are high, in contrast to decentralized settings. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for jointly managing exposure and monetization in competitive digital marketplaces.

detail.abstract:
This article presents the comprehensive global application of the PaC (Process as the Goal) Model, expanding the socio-economic theory beyond ancient Egypt to propose a universal key for understanding monumental construction projects worldwide.

For centuries, traditional interpretations of structures like the Great Pyramids, the Nazca Lines, or the statues of Easter Island have focused on religious cults or the megalomania of rulers. However, these explanations often leave a key question unanswered: Why was the societal effort so disproportionate to the visible result?. This work proposes a cohesive solution by treating these undertakings as the "Operating System" of early civilizations.

Core pillars of the Global PaC Model:

  • Universal Economic Stabilizer: In moneyless agrarian societies, massive construction projects served as standardized tools for resource management and labor mobilization.

  • The "Showroom" Effect: Analysis of "fresh" 50-ton monoliths and marketing-like displays (monumental showrooms) used to transform scattered groups into organized societies.

  • Crisis Management: Evidence suggests these projects were strategic responses to environmental instability, acting as a giant "insurance policy" against civil war and unemployment.

  • Socio-Political Utility: The construction process itself—not the finished monument—was the primary goal, serving as a tool for social integration and redistribution of food.

Empirical Evidence and Synthesis: The paper compiles 50 independent academic studies and quotations spanning various disciplines. It demonstrates that the process-as-goal logic emerges repeatedly across history, drawing a direct line from the Egyptian 4th Dynasty and the Inca Mit'a system to the modern U.S. New Deal.

By applying modern economic logic to ancient behaviors, this work serves as the empirical climax of the research series, reconciling the "absurd" cost of monumental undertakings with their practical necessity for state-building.

Its core purpose is to demonstrate the validity of the PaC theory through a rigorous analysis of thirty key pieces of evidence derived from archaeological findings, historical sources, and advanced economic modeling. The results show a unanimous consensus across all five AI models, recognizing the PaC theory as a logically sound "paradigm shift". This report recommends its inclusion in mainstream scientific research as a legitimate hypothesis for understanding early state-formation mechanisms.

title: "A Cross Country and Time Series Approach to Exploring Government Effectiveness: Bangladesh and Global Perspective."

detail.title: "A Cross Country and Time Series Approach to Exploring Government Effectiveness: Bangladesh and Global Perspective."
detail.abstract: Government effectiveness is close to equilibrium of the services it provides and the citizens' preferences. This research aims to identify the factors leading to Government effectiveness in order to provide evidence on how it is affected by the economic & educational development, political constraints, internal characteristics and public voice in the world as well as Bangladesh. For global perspective, study used cross section data of current and previous 194 member countries of the United Nations and for Bangladesh, time series covered from 1996 to 2019. OLS as well as FMOLS results reveal that, Government effectiveness is clearly associated with countries' economic & educational development, political conditions, organizational characteristics, public voice and educational budget. These are also the key indicators of worldwide good governance. In relation to the economic & educational development, World data suggests that GDP per capita and literacy rate have a strong positive correlation with Government effectiveness. On the contrary, Bangladesh exhibits an opposite result; found that a country with higher economic growth does not guarantee government effectiveness. In addition, the Government who is allocating more budgets on education leads to be an effective Government. In terms of organizational characteristics, country size (density) impedes Government effectiveness especially true for Bangladesh. On the other hand, in countries with lower political constraints, the executive can change the policies, when it desires, thus, citizens can get their desired outcomes. It can be concluded that, voice and accountability comprised of freedom, political rights, participation in the selection of Governments and independence of media positively bolster Government effectiveness.

detail.abstract: The global transition into the Sovereign AI Moment (SAM) represents a profound civilizational and technological juncture. Classical paradigms of governance are currently collapsing under the weight of algorithmic acceleration and environmental extraction. To deliver a definitive, holistic diagnosis of structural power, we must transcend siloed technical assessments and evaluate the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) through a macro-systemic framework. This manuscript represents a theoretical and architectural intervention of unique magnitude across political economy, the sociology of technology, and complex systems theory. Contextualized by Edgar Morin, we recognize the 4IR as a "polycrisis"-a highly entangled network where ecological, technological, and political realities are inextricably linked. For society to transcend the extractive, meaning-blind algorithms of surveillance capitalism, a rigorous epistemological foundation is required. By synthesizing infrastructural realities with psychoanalytic principles, this essay maps the crisis across the "Seven Axes of the World," guided by the semiotic progression of Code (1) → Meaning (2) → Action (3).

detail.title: From Lender of Last Resort to Pawnbroker for All Seasons: A Critical Analysis of Central Bank Liquidity Intervention and the Limits of King's PFAS Proposal
detail.abstract: This article critically examines the evolving role of central banks as liquidity providers in modern financial systems, with particular focus on Mervyn King's proposal that central banks should operate as a "Pawnbroker for All Seasons" (PFAS). Traditionally conceptualised as lenders of last resort, central banks have increasingly intervened earlier and more extensively in response to systemic crises, particularly following the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. This shift has prompted calls for a more structured and pre-emptive liquidity framework. Through doctrinal and economic analysis, this article evaluates the theoretical foundations, practical implications, and systemic risks associated with King's proposal. It argues that while the PFAS model offers a compelling attempt to address liquidity fragility and moral hazard, it introduces significant challenges relating to feasibility, procyclicality, collateral constraints, and institutional legitimacy. The article concludes that reforming existing liquidity frameworks, rather than adopting a radical restructuring of central banking functions, provides a more coherent and sustainable response to financial instability.

title: Plant disease pandemics must occupy centre stage of global food security

detail.title: Plant disease pandemics must occupy centre stage of global food security
detail.abstract: Diseases affecting plants have been feared as much as human diseases and war throughout the history of mankind. A single race of a plant pathogen can spread chilling effects down the spine of human race. Yet deep impact of plant diseases causing monumental losses to humankind has not attracted attention the international community as much as human diseases. Even viruliferous scar inflicted by plant disease pandemics on global economy in all regions of the planet has never evoked as much empathy of humankind as human disease pandemics such as recent Covid-19 pandemic. Even though plant diseases eat away one third of the slice of the global food cake causing a significant dent in the food security scenario, it seems the world turns away its eyes eerily from this dreaded menace. Plant health contributes directly to many of the sustainable development goals (SDGs) we ought to achieve by 2030. Enemies of plant health just don't stop at a nation's borders, and thousands of miles of oceans can't prevent spread of the plant diseases and pests either. The recent examples are wheat blast disease and banana Fusarium wilt disease. Forces are to join hands, integrated at the global scale to defeat unforeseen plant disease outbreaks on the world's agricultural landscapes, thereby ensuring global food security at all levels in every nook and corner of the globe. On one hand, we need to increase food production by 60% from current level to feed the burgeoning global population; on the other, world contribution to the research budget on combating plant disease pandemics is too meagre in comparison to human disease pandemics such as acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) or Covid-19. For example, the US budget for research on human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) causing AIDS was US$2.6 billion in 2020, and that was US$150 million more than the entire budget for agricultural research. Research on plant disease pandemics supported by a budget commensurate to that of human disease pandemics would be just befitting to fight the scourge of hunger and famine. And plant disease pandemics ought to receive buzzword status across the globe through extensive media coverage. #PlantDiseasePandemic should trend in social media platforms at international level to focus it on the lime light. Sparks need to fly instigating the very idea of dominating global media headlines by this ruthlessly neglected yet extremely vital domain, i.e., plant disease pandemics vis-à-vis food security. This is all the more important in the present conflict-ridden world when armed conflicts are at historic high, engulfing fertile agricultural lands forcing humankind to produce more with less in order to overcome conflict-induced food insecurity!

detail.abstract: Human-like AI is rapidly reshaping higher education. Students start using these tools with anthropomorphic features to write and study, while faculty uses them for lectures, grading, and advising. However, its governance remains underdeveloped and inconsistent when it comes to harms caused during this transformation of learning, teaching, and research experiences on campus. Currently, U.S. institutions regulate these tools in fragmented, polycentric ways, typically choosing between prohibitive, laissez-faire, or constructive approaches; but they often rely on informal norms and vague ethical guidance, which undermined institutional trust. By analyzing the problem with Elinor Ostrom’s Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework to education-related legal disputes and focuses on law and policy solutions, this article found that absent of a comprehensive federal or state regulation, direct communication is essential to rebuild trust via Ostrom’s trust-reciprocity-reputation triangle, and suggests that a constructive, trust-centered policy governance approach will help rebuild trust on campus and advance AI innovation with responsible risk management.

title: Navigating the Predictive Self: Metastyling as Architecture of Stabilizable Identity Configurations
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Navigating the Predictive Self: Metastyling as Architecture of Stabilizable Identity Configurations
detail.abstract: The predictive processing account of selfhood-developed by Seth (Being You, 2021), Friston (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2010), Damasio (Self Comes to Mind, 2010), and Varela, Thompson and Rosch (The Embodied Mind, 1991)-establishes that identity is a dynamic biological construction: a generative model continuously updated through interoceptive inference and active engagement with an uncertain environment. This account provides a compelling mechanistic description of how the self is produced, but it does not supply an architecture of the configurations the predictive self can occupy: a formalization of stable identity states, the topology of movement between them, and the structural conditions under which intentional navigation of that topology becomes possible. This paper proposes that the Metastyling framework (Pau, 2025) provides precisely this architecture. We argue that stable identity configurations-designated Faces-function as attractor basins in a high-dimensional predictive landscape, characterized by DMES state vectors (Direction, Meaning, Expression, State) and indexed by attractor depth parameter β, which corresponds formally to the precision-weighting of the configuration's prior beliefs in Friston's active inference framework. Transition Cost between configurations is formalized as a function of attractor depth, configurational distance, meta-cognitive capacity, and transition time-an operationalization of the free energy expenditure required for identity model revision. Levels of Awareness (LoA) are introduced as the trainable meta-cognitive capacity that modulates the organism's relationship to its own prediction error, determining the range of navigational agency available at any moment. Together, these constructs constitute a topological account of identity that dissolves the opposition between essentialist and constructionist models, explains the structural resistance to identity change, and generates testable predictions at physiological, behavioral, and developmental levels.

title: The Ludic Operator: Play Modality, Curiosity, and the Reduction of Identity Transition Cost

detail.abstract: Contemporary subjects face a structural asymmetry: the conditions that demand navigational flexibility-institutional acceleration, dissolving social scripts, proliferating identity options-are precisely the conditions that make identity transition most costly. The Metastyling Framework formalises this cost through a Cost Function whose alignment parameter α determines whether transition cost scales linearly or exponentially. This paper addresses a question the Cost Function raises but does not answer: what shifts in the navigator's operational mode make transitions that were previously prohibitive become traversable? We propose that ludic modality-a mode of engaging with identity configurations in which Face activation is framed as hypothesis rather than commitment-functions as a structural operator on α, formalised through a new parameter γ (the ludic coefficient). When γ > 0, the perceived stake structure of Face activation is modified without altering attractor depth, configurational distance, or navigation efficiency; cost scaling shifts from exponential toward linear, and the State vector stabilises before the system generates the coherence-crisis response that makes imposed transitions prohibitive. We review the ludic tradition in identity theory-Winnicott's potential space, Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, Suits's lusory attitudeand show that these accounts converged on the same phenomenon without formalising the mechanism that γ specifies.

title: The Double Edge of Freedom of Contract
affiliations: and University of Minnesota - Law School

detail.title: The Double Edge of Freedom of Contract
detail.abstract: Standard economic reasoning suggests that expanding an individual's choice set cannot reduce welfare because additional options may always be ignored. This intuition underlies the traditional economic justification for freedom of contract. This paper shows that the monotonic relationship between choice and welfare may break down in bargaining environments characterized by asymmetric bilateral monopoly and unequal costs of disagreement. In such settings, some contractual options do not improve the weaker party's outside alternative but instead expand the set of concessions that the stronger party can credibly demand during negotiation. The paper introduces a distinction between beneficial options, which strengthen a party's disagreement position, and leverage options, which enlarge the bargaining space without improving the weaker party's exit opportunities. When leverage options become legally available, the bargaining equilibrium may shift in favor of the stronger party, even if the options themselves are never exercised. The analysis suggests that certain legal limits on contractual autonomy-such as doctrines of public policy, duress, abuse of dependence, and unconscionability-can be understood as institutional commitment devices that remove leverage options from the bargaining space. Rather than imposing paternalistic limits on voluntary exchange, these rules can be understood as providing bargaining safeguards in relationships marked by asymmetric bargaining power. A comparative analysis of legal systems, together with a range of illustrative case studies spanning family, employment, and commercial relationships, shows how legal institutions frequently operate in this manner. The paper thus offers a unified explanation for a wide range of limits on contractual freedom and identifies conditions under which restricting contractual options may improve the welfare of vulnerable parties.

title: Why the Federal Reserve Cuts Rates when Public Debt Rises
affiliations: and Northwestern University

detail.title: Why the Federal Reserve Cuts Rates when Public Debt Rises
detail.abstract: We document a new fact: conditional on inflation and output, the Federal Reserve lowers the policy rate when the U.S. public debt-to-GDP ratio increases. To explain this pattern, we develop and estimate a New Keynesian model with shocks to households' demand for public debt. These shocks generate a negative comovement between public debt and the natural rate, defined as the real interest rate that would prevail under flexible prices. Assuming that the Federal Reserve adjusts its policy rate in line with the natural rate, the model rationalizes the negative relationship between debt and the policy rate. Two complementary exercises support this mechanism. First, we show that shocks to the demand for public debt are a key driver of business cycle fluctuations. Second, we construct a debt-informed measure of the natural rate using a time-varying parameter vector autoregression. When this measure is included in the policy rule, an increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio no longer reduces the policy rate.

title: What moves households’ expectations during a crisis? Evidence from a randomized information experiment

detail.title: What moves households’ expectations during a crisis? Evidence from a randomized information experiment
detail.abstract: We investigate households’ economic expectations at the onset of the COVID-19 crisis, using a randomized information experiment within a representative survey. Households that receive information about experts’ views become more pessimistic and uncertain regarding future output growth and are less willing to consume. This effect also applies to households informed about major monetary and fiscal stimulus measures, revealing that the negative outlook from policy announcements overshadows the intended positive effects of these measures. The effects persist for at least one month after the treatment. Households less affected by the pandemic, either through financial losses or limited news exposure, are initially less pessimistic and react more strongly to the treatments. The results underscore the key role of personal experience in expectation formation and suggest that inattention is pervasive among households, even during a once-in-a-lifetime crisis.

detail.abstract: We explore to what extent real returns on investment portfolios can be hedged against inflation risk by using existing financial market instruments. We empirically find that inflation-linked bonds offer only limited protection against inflation risk, while nominal debt and stocks play at least comparable roles in this respect. The demonstrated limits of hedging inflation risk are of particular relevance for long-term investors, such as pension funds with participants concerned about the real value of their pension benefits.

title: Accommodating Age

detail.title: Accommodating Age
detail.abstract: This Article reimagines employment discrimination law with respect to age. Currently, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) prohibits discrimination solely on the basis of chronological age, while the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) protects certain workers with impairments or disabilities linked to physiological age. This framework leaves a gap: it does not protect workers who face discrimination or workplace challenges due to differences stemming from their cohort age-their generational placement, which shapes shared social, cultural, and historical experiences, as well as members' values, attitudes, and interests. To fill this gap, the Article proposes a four-part framework to transform age discrimination law. First, it would expand the definition of age to include cohort age, recognizing a broader range of age-related harms. Second, it would require employers to reasonably accommodate age cohort effects, enabling workers to remain productively employed for as long as they are willing and able. Third, to implement a reciprocity principle, the framework would incorporate an accrual-based accommodation model: new hires would initially receive only minimal accommodations, with entitlements increasing with tenure. Fourth, because the justifications for the ADEA's minimum age threshold do not apply to an accommodation mandate for age cohort effects, and because younger workers would significantly benefit from such a mandate, the framework would eliminate that threshold for asserting accommodation claims.

title: Do Alternative Livelihoods Reduce Resource Pressure? Evidence from Tourism and Fisheries in the Galapagos
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Charles Darwin Foundation and Charles Darwin Foundation

detail.title: Do Alternative Livelihoods Reduce Resource Pressure? Evidence from Tourism and Fisheries in the Galapagos
detail.abstract: Developing alternative economic sectors is widely promoted as a strategy to reduce pressure on natural resources while improving livelihoods, yet opportunities to rigorously evaluate whether diversification reduces harvesting pressure are rare. We provide such an evaluation using unique linked data on tourism, artisanal fisheries, prices, and fisher occupations from the Galapagos Islands. We develop a resource-economic model in which both resource prices and the opportunity cost of harvesting depend on the development of tourism as a non-resource sector. The model predicts that harvesting declines only when wages in the alternative sector rise more rapidly than resource profitability; otherwise aggregate effort is maintained and re-allocated across resources toward those with higher marginal profitability. Calibration using observed wage and price responses indicates that diversification primarily induces within-sector reallocation rather than exit from harvesting. We test these predictions using the tourism ban implemented during the COVID-19 lockdown in the Galapagos as a policy-induced negativedemand shock. Because fisheries were explicitly exempted, the ban created a sector-specific shutdown in which tourism ceased while fishing continued, generating a natural field experiment. Tourism substantially raises fishers’ revenue by increasing local prices, yet the decline in tourism did not reduce aggregate landings. Instead, effort shifted toward more profitable fisheries, moving extraction away from endemic and biologically vulnerable species toward healthier stocks. Dual-sector fishers expanded effort while single-sector fishers reduced it. Diversification toward a non-resource sector can thus generate income gains while inducing environmental losses by reshaping harvesting incentives rather than reducing extraction.

detail.title: Comprehensive evaluation of typical medical waste treatment technologies in view of environmental and economic perspectives
detail.abstract: The outbreak of COVID-19 has caused a sharp increase in the amount of medical waste (MW), which is infectious and harmful to the environment and human body. However, existing MW disposal methods face challenges in achieving high treatment efficiency, and creates an urgent need for more cost-effective and environmentally friendly technologies. In this research, a comprehensive evaluation, including comprehensive environment assessment (CEA), life cycle assessment (LCA), and economic assessment (EA), was proposed for three typical MW treatment methodologies (i.e., in situ friction heat treatment technology, chemical disinfection, and microwave sterilization). Results showed that the in situ friction heat treatment had the minimal environmental impact with CEA score of 5509.11, whereas the chemical disinfection technology had the highest value of 69384.62. In terms of LCA, microwave sterilization had a relatively low global warming potential (GWP) (6.01 E+02 kg CO2 eq). From the EA perspective, chemical disinfection technology emerged as the most economically viable option, costing merely 29.64% of that of microwave sterilization. After environment-economy integration analysis, in situ friction heat treatment technology emerged as the best disposal method, which had a relatively low pollution emissions and reasonable cost among the three technologies. This study can serve as a guidance for treating MW in a more environmentally friendly and economical way in the future.

title: Another Reason for Non-Neutrality of Financial Liquidity

detail.title: Another Reason for Non-Neutrality of Financial Liquidity
detail.abstract: This paper reinterprets the non-neutrality of financial liquidity under a general equilibrium model with multiple financial liquidities, but without price stickiness. Non-neutrality opens the possibility of effective monetary or financial policy on the crisis-prone real economy and thus revisiting its nature is worthwhile. We find that models with only one asset and money limit our perspectives to see the nature of financial liquidities interacting with real economy. Departing from abstracting an economy with only one interest rate allows us to see the underlying reason of non-neutrality of financial liquidities, that is, industry-specific rates of return distinguishable from the representative rate of return. Without the assumption of price stickiness but with a wider frame of multiple liquidities, this paper offers another reason for non-neutrality of financial liquidity and naturally clarifies the meaning of money neutrality. We incorporate complicated reality of multiple financial liquidities in a theoretical model, which is a way of deepening our understanding of financial market.

detail.title: Beyond the Blueprint: Empirical Insights on Survey-to-Survey Imputation in Peru
detail.abstract: This paper empirically validates several survey-to-survey (S2S) imputation methods, focusing on their performance during structural shocks, using household survey data from Peru from 2010–2022. While these methods deliver high accuracy in stable periods, their predictive power declines sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic. A decomposition analysis shows that failures arise primarily from fundamental shifts in the relationship between household characteristics and welfare, rather than from changes in unobservable factors. Incorporating variables strongly associated with consumption-based welfare, such as labor income and government transfers, can partially mitigate prediction errors during crises. However, cross-country validations with data from Mongolia and Georgia reveal that the effectiveness of these predictors is highly context-dependent. These findings underscore a critical challenge: variables most predictive during crises are often unavailable in non-consumption surveys, precisely when S2S imputation is most needed. The paper highlights the importance of understanding local contexts and setting realistic expectations for model performance under structural change.

detail.abstract: This Article extends the voluntary compliance framework developed in Can the Public Be Trusted? The Promise and Perils of Voluntary Compliance to the corporate context. While recent scholarship has explored when states can rely on non-coercive regulatory approaches with individual citizens, comparatively little attention has been paid to whether these insights translate to business entities. This Article argues that corporations present both greater challenges and greater opportunities for voluntary compliance regimes. On one hand, the instrumental orientation of corporate decision-making, amplified by fiduciary duties and competitive pressures, may systematically undermine the intrinsic motivations that voluntary compliance frameworks depend upon. Drawing on behavioral ethics research, demonstrating that organizational settings can serve as “hotbeds for unethicality,” this Article identifies structural features of corporate environments that impede genuine voluntary compliance. On the other hand, corporations possess characteristics that facilitate trust-based regulation: they are repeat players sensitive to reputational consequences, operate through transparent bureaucratic processes amenable to monitoring, and cannot claim violations of personal autonomy when past behavior informs regulatory treatment. This Article synthesizes these competing considerations into a differentiated framework for corporate regulation, identifying the conditions under which non-coercive approaches are most likely to succeed across securities regulation, environmental compliance, and corporate governance more broadly.

title: Should Antitrust Pursue Multiple Policy Goals?
affiliations: International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE) and Cornell University - Law School

detail.title: Should Antitrust Pursue Multiple Policy Goals?
detail.abstract:
Some scholars argue that antitrust should abandon the consumer welfare standard and adopt a "welfare dashboard" that considers not just competition, but all social values that antitrust could possibly influence, including democracy, inequality, and small business protection. Recently, some advocates of this approach have argued that it is firmly grounded in modern economics. As we explain, the opposite is true. Economic policy research virtually never employs broad welfare frameworks like this because they are unworkable. Among other problems, resolving tradeoffs between diverse phenomena like competition and democracy requires assigning them "welfare weights" that no one knows how to specify. The sheer impracticality of this approach means that it inevitably collapses into subjective speculation. 

While consumer welfare has well-known limitations, most of them are minor in single-market antitrust analysis, and those that remain can be addressed using better methods to measure welfare. A key benefit of consumer welfare is that it provides a sensible means of aggregating the different variables associated with competition (e.g. price and quality) using observable data, without requiring subjective welfare weights. In antitrust's adversarial system, this provides a shared normative framework for resolving policy disagreements objectively. By contrast, a dashboard allows each side to assert different (often incommensurable) normative values with no way to resolve the conflict.

title: Assessing Rwanda's National Electrification Strategy: Impact and Trade-offs
affiliations: University of Seville, University of Stirling, Universidad Loyola Andalucía and University of Stirling - Department of Accounting and Finance

detail.title: Assessing Rwanda's National Electrification Strategy: Impact and Trade-offs
detail.abstract: Like many African countries, Rwanda faces challenges with high biomass reliance and low electricity access, impeding sustainable development. To address this, the 2016 National Electrification Strategy (NES) was launched, promoting both on-grid and off-grid renewable solutions. This study assesses the impact of the NES on electricity access, renewable energy consumption share, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions using the Synthetic Control Method (SCM). The key findings reveal a multifaceted outcome: the NES significantly boosted electricity access by approximately 17 percentage points. However, it led to a decrease in the share of renewable energy consumption by more than 4 percentage points. Total GHG emissions exceed the synthetic control by about 1070 kilotons of CO 2 equivalent. These results highlight crucial trade-offs between rapid electrification and environmental sustainability. Robustness checks confirm our findings. The study provides valuable quantitative evidence on the complex outcomes of a major electrification policy in a developing economy. The results underscore the critical need for integrated policy frameworks that simultaneously pursue electrification goals while implementing measures to preserve renewable energy usage and mitigate adverse environmental impacts, offering insights for policymakers seeking to balance these objectives.

detail.abstract: Obtaining a law degree from an ABA-approved law school has long been the primary path into the American legal profession. However, some states have alternative educational pathways, including earning a law degree from a non-ABA-approved law school or completing supervised legal study. Using data from 1984 and 2019, we investigate the track record of these alternative pathways into the legal profession. We find that alternative pathways have been available at some point in all but 11 states, raising questions about the extent to which the ABA's gatekeeping role exerts anti-competitive control over entry into the profession. However, we also find that individuals with alternative legal training pass the bar exam at drastically lower rates than graduates of ABA-approved law schools. This disparity persists across every state, demonstrating states' inability to regulate alternative pathways effectively. Moreover, we find that lawyers with alternative legal training have meaningfully worse career outcomes and pose a greater risk to the public than other lawyers, which may help explain why alternative pathways have not taken off as a more prominent mode of legal training.

title: The Periodic Topology of Risk (TPTR): Escaping the Regulatory Matrix via Chronopotency
affiliations: Global Central Banking Risk, Global Central Banking Risk and Global Central Banking Risk

detail.title: The Periodic Topology of Risk (TPTR): Escaping the Regulatory Matrix via Chronopotency
detail.abstract: The banking collapses of 2023 exposed a fatal divergence between regulatory compliance and kinetic reality. This paper argues that the global financial architecture has succumbed to "The Matrix Dilemma": a state where institutions optimize for a simulated environment of static capital ratios (Risk-Weighted Assets), while decoupling from the high-velocity physics of modern liquidity runs. We introduce the Periodic Topology of Risk (TPTR) to map this disconnect, identifying two primary failure mechanisms: (1) The Titanic Theorem, which mathematically demonstrates that as organizational mass expands, the institution's "Chronomic Turning Radius" inevitably exceeds the velocity of crisis evolution; and (2) The Trojan Asset Hypothesis, which reveals how accounting treatments (Hold-to-Maturity) allow structurally safe but temporally toxic securities to bypass risk perimeters. To counteract these forces, we propose a paradigm shift from static resilience to Chronopotency (Temporal Sovereignty). A chronopotent institution is defined not by its capital buffer size, but by its ability to synchronize its decision-loops with the accelerating speed of digital bank runs. By integrating concepts from kinematic physics and Baudrillardian simulation theory into Working Paper Series | February 2026 2 financial risk management, this study provides a new topological map for engineering systems that do not merely survive volatility, but weaponize time against it.

detail.abstract: This paper reviews the process of structural transformation (ST) across a wide range of Asian economies. After outlining key theories of ST, it documents Asia’s transformation and compares it with patterns observed elsewhere, using standard indicators and broader dimensions of structural change. It then examines the contribution of ST to productivity growth, drawing on disaggregated data. Finally, it assesses whether Asian economies exhibit signs of premature deindustrialization. The findings show that Asia’s ST broadly mirrors global experience but features a steeper decline in agriculture and faster expansion of services as income rises. Structural transformation has contributed positively to productivity growth, largely through labor reallocation out of agriculture. Agriculture shows the largest productivity gaps relative to the United States, while services show the smallest, suggesting substantial productivity gains from labor shifts toward services. There is no evidence of premature deindustrialization; industrial shares of output and inputs have not declined with higher incomes.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the consequences of community banks modifying their lending to avoid crossing asset size thresholds that trigger increases in reporting, audit, and governance requirements. Using a sample of 6,841 bank-quarter observations and over 761,000 loan-level records from 2012–2024, we document significant bunching of community banks just below these asset thresholds. Unlike large banks that adjust investment portfolios, community banks manage size by rejecting loans that are typically associated with relationship lending, in particular, small business loans and personal loans to underserved populations (such as minorities and lower income households). Consistent with reduced lending having real effects, we find that counties with community banks that are just below the threshold see a decline in new business formation and decreasing wages. Our evidence suggests that size-based regulation motivates some community banks to retreat from aspects of their traditional relationship lending role, with effects on local economic outcomes and underserved communities.

detail.title: Memories of the Stock Market
detail.abstract: Factors such as personality or sentiment can color both recall and expectations across individuals and thus induce spurious associations between the two. Fortunately, it is a hallmark of (faulty) memory that a refresher can correct it. This makes it possible to isolate the causal within-subject link. In a survey here, respondents were asked to recall the 2025 and 2020-2025 S&P 500 market rates of return. They were also asked for expected rates of return before and after they were shown the correct historical values. The results provide strong evidence that memory plays a central role. Furthermore, memory correction worked not only through changing recall and expected returns, but also through changing "typical return" assessments.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of illicit mining operations within the South Africa's extractive industries, particularly in Orkney located in Northwest Province has emerged as a pressing socioeconomic and law enforcement concern. Recent intervention of the South African Police Service (SAPS) regarding operation "Vala umgodi" (seal the holes) have sought to disrupt subterranean networks by obstructing supply routes used to sustain unauthorised miners operating underground. In light of these developments, this study investigates the lived experiences of illicit miners and critically examines the operational strategies employed by the SAPS to mitigate illicit mining activities. The research is situated within the broader context of systematic youth unemployment, which has contributed to the entrenchment of informal and illicit economic practices among marginalized populations. A qualitative research design was adopted to facilitate nuanced inquiry into the phenomenon. Purposive sampling enabled the selection of law enforcement personnel directly engaged in anti-illicit mining operations, while snowball sampling was employed to access dispersed networks of illicit miners and elicit their perspectives. Data collection was conducted through semi structured interviews, allowing for rich contextualised insights into both enforcement challenges and the socioeconomic drivers of illicit mining activities. This study further disclosed that illicit miners are educated human being who came to south Africa with the purpose of finding greener pastures, of major concern is that there are different groups of illicit miners who also wants to partake in illicit mining activities. Illicit miners are constantly burnt to death underground due to lack knowledge on how to use chemicals. Likewise, police official and red dot trained security personnel often retrieved charcoaled bodies with no heads, arms, and legs. The study further discovered that law enforcers often traumatised by such issues and some further attends employee health and wellness (EHW) to receive counselling. The major concerns from law enforcers are that illicit miners came to South Africa illegally and it is extremely problematic to trace family members of the illicit miners. The study also revealed that the address given to police officials is not valid, thus situation further led to the government to organise pauper funeral for all illicit miners. The findings of the study reveal that participants engaged in mineral extraction often resorting to reopening sealed shafts through explosive means. The study further identifies a nexus between illicit mining and broader patterns of criminality underscoring the complexity of underground economies in post-industrial mining regions. The article therefore recommend that illicit activities should be legalised, and new legislative should be formulated with the aim of supporting illicit miners.

detail.abstract: Renowned for its pseudonymity and decentralized nature, virtual asset technology has emerged as a felicitous avenue for money launderers. In response to the anti-money laundering (AML) risks associated with this nascent technology, the international money laundering 'watchdog' known as the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has recently provided specific guidance for regulators in each country to implement. While this guidance provides a strong base framework, there are three core challenges that regulators will face in their implementation of this guidance: (a) bureaucratic delay, (b) regulatory arbitrage, and (c) industry pushback. This article suggests that any research pertaining to virtual asset regulation, especially within the context of international AML efforts, should directly address these challenges head-on. It is important to keep these topics top-of-mind, such that regulatory efforts are most effectively designed, and the "big picture" is not missed. By directly addressing the challenges discussed in this article-along with the broad suggestions to mitigate each of these challenges-regulators will be able to effectively mitigate the AML risks associated with virtual asset technology in compliance with the newest FATF guidance.

detail.abstract: In automobile markets where consumers attach social recognition to car ownership, how does the introduction of a lower-cost alternative influence the market outcomes of traditional internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs)? Leveraging high-frequency sales data covering China's entire automobile market from 2018 to 2022, we examine heterogeneous market responses to the emergence of electric vehicles (EVs) across different price segments. Overall, the rise of EVs is associated with lower ICEV sales but higher total automobile sales. More importantly, while EV penetration is negatively correlated with ICEV sales in the lowand mid-end segments, it is positively correlated with ICEV sales in the high-end segment. Further evidence suggests that the rise of EVs amplifies the symbolic value of high-end ICEVs, boosting sales of ICEV models with strong social recognition.

detail.abstract: The Improvement Scope Adjusted for Sample (ISAS) is defined as the empirical improvement vector D = C • 1 n-I, where I = Xw is the PCA-weighted achievement index, C = m ⊤ w is the empirical ceiling (weighted sample maxima), X ∈ R n×p is the min-max normalized data matrix (n = 175 observations, p = 6 indicators with 30 subindicators), S is the sample covariance, and w pca maximizes Var(I) = w ⊤ Sw subject to 1 ⊤ w = 1, w ≥ 0. We show that PCA-weighted ISAS satisfies the key properties of empowerment indices from Kabeer (1999), who conceptualised empowerment as a multi-dimensional process encompassing resources (preconditions), agency (decision-making processes), and achievements (outcomes), with measures requiring indivisibility, contextuality, and sensitivity to power dynamics. ISAS aligns by capturing relative distances to an empirical, context-specific frontier, maximising variance thorough PCA to reflect underlying correlations in the sample data. Additionally, as proven in the main text (Propositions 1-2, Sufficient Condition), ISAS is appropriate for small samples (n = 175), with level-sensitivity to observed maxima while retaining stable rankings and high variance.

detail.abstract: To the author's knowledge, no general architecture exists for taxing wealth on a third-party-verifiable, no-filing basis across multiple claim classes. This paper constructs one for covered non-nominal claims. It embeds a well-established mechanism from the property-rights literature — that agents voluntarily formalize claims because registration raises claim value (de Soto 2000; Arruñada 2003, 2012) — in a model with taxation. The compliance margin studied by Allingham and Sandmo (1972) — continuous self-reporting within the system — is replaced by a participation margin: whether to enter the covered base at all. Under a reserve-decomposition benchmark, this margin is binary and threshold-based; the non-covered reserve is bounded; and the registered share converges to full coverage at scale within verification-dominant claim classes. The architecture delivers four core properties: endogenous participation into the covered base, asymptotic coverage within verification-dominant claim classes, automatic assessment from registry and intermediary data, and intermediary collection without taxpayer filing, self-reporting, calculation, or remittance. The architecture is non-consolidated by design, taxing distinct covered claims claim-by-claim rather than consolidated net worth. Because the base is endogenous, the government faces a rate-versus-coverage trade-off; the paper characterizes the interior revenue-maximizing rate and shows that the elasticity of the endogenous base equals one at the optimum.

detail.title: Are Stablecoins and Bank Deposits Substitutes?
detail.abstract: We test whether stablecoins and bank deposits act as substitutes. Using local projections fit to weekly U.S. data from January 2019 to June 2025, we find that deposit rate increases predict slower stablecoin market capitalization growth. To address endogeneity, we exploit a nonlinearity in deposit rate pass-through. Unlike other money market rates, banks reprice deposits more aggressively once the federal funds rate exceeds approximately 3%. Against average ten-week stablecoin growth of 15%, ordinary least squares estimates imply a reduction of roughly 3 percentage points per basis point of deposit repricing, while instrumental variable estimates are roughly three times larger and pass a bitcoin placebo test. Effects are stronger for Circle's USDC than for Tether's USDT, consistent with USDC's closer ties to U.S. depositors. Cross-sectional variation in repricing across deposit tiers provides independent supporting evidence of substitution.

detail.abstract: This educational paper develops a practical movement taxonomy for belly dance as an adapted, low-impact, culturally meaningful movement modality for adult wellness, healthy aging, and functional fitness. The paper is literature-based and does not report new human-subject data. Instead, it synthesizes belly-dance-specific studies and the broader dance-and-aging literature to propose a structured framework for class design, movement selection, progression, and safety screening. The rationale for this project is twofold. First, the published evidence suggests that dance interventions can improve physical function, mobility, balance, quality of life, and selected psychosocial outcomes in middle-aged and older adults, although effect sizes vary across genres, doses, and populations. Second, belly dance possesses distinctive movement features segmental trunk control, multiplanar pelvic articulation, rhythmic weight transfer, expressive upper-limb patterning, and scalable intensity that make it particularly suitable for adaptation across adult skill levels. Belly-dance-specific evidence is still limited, yet randomized and controlled studies have reported improvements in pain, functional capacity, selfimage, depressive symptoms, range of motion, and selected pelvic-floor-related outcomes in specific female populations. Building on this literature, the present paper proposes a five-domain movement taxonomy: postural organization, locomotor weight transfer, pelvic articulation, trunk and thoracic mobility, and expressive integration. Each domain is translated into pedagogical guidance for screening, dosing, cueing, progression, and modification in community and educational settings. The paper also presents implementation principles for beginners aged 40+, deconditioned adults, and mixed-level community classes. The central argument is not that belly dance should be framed as a medical treatment, but that it deserves recognition as an adherence-friendly, body-positive, functionally relevant movement practice that can be taught safely and systematically. The framework is intended for use on educational platforms and by instructors seeking academically grounded guidance for adult classes.

detail.abstract:
This article serves as a comprehensive defense and "stress-test" of the Process as the Goal (PaC) Model. By proactively identifying and addressing ten key points of skepticism, the author bridges the gap between traditional Egyptological interpretations and a modern socio-economic framework.

The central aim is to verify the internal logic and resilience of the PaC theory. It provides a transparent tool for rigorous scholarly debate, moving beyond the religious-vs-economic dichotomy to offer a hierarchy of causality for the Great Pyramids of Egypt.

Key issues addressed in this polemical analysis include:

  1. The Efficiency Paradox: Resolving why "wasteful" monumental construction was an economically rational choice.

  2. Anachronism vs. Analogy: Validating the use of modern economic tools to analyze ancient state strategies.

  3. The Role of Religion: Clarifying religion as a legitimizing "operating system" for state economic goals.

  4. Strategic Maturity: Explaining why the phasing out of pyramid-building actually proves the model's success.

  5. Measuring Intangibles: Methods for quantifying social stability and national integration.

This FAQ is a critical component of the author’s ongoing research series, providing the methodological and polemical foundation necessary for a deeper understanding of monumental architecture as a state-driven tool for national development.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation fundamentally changes how organizations create value and impact society, giving rise to Corporate Digital Responsibility (CDR) as a distinct dimension of corporate responsibility. This study explores whether digital responsibility initiatives shape stakeholder preferences differently compared to traditional Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). Building on the theoretical foundations of signaling theory, social identity theory, and expectation-disconfirmation theory, we propose that CDR generates stronger stakeholder preferences than CSR due to unique characteristics of digital technologies. Additionally, we examine whether opportunity-based CDR (leveraging technology for societal benefit) outperforms risk-based CDR (mitigating digital harms). Through a vignette experiment with 150 participants evaluating scenarios as customers or prospective employees, we uncover unexpected results: when effectiveness is equal, stakeholders show no preference for CDR over CSR, with customers even significantly favoring traditional CSR initiatives. Furthermore, the distinction between opportunitybased and risk-based CDR does not influence preferences either. These findings suggest that stakeholders primarily evaluate responsibility initiatives based on their tangible outcomes rather than their technological sophistication. The study contributes to the emerging CDR literature by demonstrating that despite conceptual distinctions, stakeholders may not perceive digital responsibility as fundamentally different from traditional CSR in their behavioral responses. For practitioners, this implies that demonstrating the realworld impact of their actions should be prioritized over highlighting their digital mode.

title: Antecedents, Decisions and Outcomes of Real Estate Auctions: A Systematic Literature Review
affiliations: University of Navarra, University of Navarra, University of Navarra - School of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Antecedents, Decisions and Outcomes of Real Estate Auctions: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract:
This paper provides the first comprehensive systematic review of the real estate auction literature since Quan (1994), analyzing 92 empirical and theoretical studies published between 1990 and 2025. Applying the Antecedents-Decisions-Outcomes framework alongside PRISMA guidelines, we document that extant research is characterized by a "narrow funnel" architecture, where a concentrated set of contextual drivers shapes a limited range of strategic choices, ultimately resulting in price-centric outcomes. While bidder heterogeneity and institutional settings are frequently examined, property type and technology remain analytically peripheral. We use tripartite network and co-occurrence analysis to show that the persistent dominance of price-centric outcomes systematically reflects a narrow analytical framing concentrated on auction type and market conditions, rather than representing their universal causal primacy. 

We document an evolutionary shift from descriptive OLS-based associations to advanced causal identification strategies, including Heckman selection models, instrumental variables, and quasi-natural experiments. Our network analysis uncovers two primary transmission mechanisms linking market context to performance, namely information disclosure and seller pricing. Strategy is the critical brokerage node mediating behavioral outcomes such as the winner's curse. We identify critical gaps in the integration of technological and behavioral dimensions, noting that digital platforms remain understudied despite their market prevalence. Based on our findings, we argue that machine learning and blockchain applications are two promising topics for further research.

title: Effect of Employment Protection on Domestic Violence

detail.title: Effect of Employment Protection on Domestic Violence
detail.abstract: This paper documents the effects of employment protections for victims of domestic violence as established by California's Senate Bill 400 implemented in January 2014 on the reporting of intimate partner violence. Results indicate that rates of intimate partner violence reports increased by 14 percent following the enactment of the law. This appears to be primarily driven by Black and Hispanic victims. Further, the increase is concentrated in tracts with higher unemployment rate and poverty rate as well as non-White and renter population, and those with below median income and education. Arrests for intimate partner violence also rose, driven by felony rather than misdemeanor cases, while 911 calls for domestic abuse remained unchangedconsistent with increased reporting rather than higher incidence. These findings suggest that strengthening job-retention rights for victims can lower the economic costs of disclosure, improve engagement with formal institutions, and reduce disparities in reporting across communities.

title: Climate News Betas and Risk Premia

detail.title: Climate News Betas and Risk Premia
detail.abstract: We investigate whether climate risk, as captured by news-based betas, is priced in U.S. and Chinese stocks. Crucially, we measure how sensitive this pricing is to common methodological variations. We estimate 144 distinct climate news betas for each stock by varying the climate news index, data frequency (daily vs. monthly), estimation window length, climate index transformation, and control variables. Our results reveal substantial sampling as well as methodological variation in beta estimates. Only about 6-10% of the long-short portfolios based on climate betas yield statistically significant premia, either positive or negative. After correcting for multiple testing, none remain significant. These findings highlight that methodological choices significantly affect both climate betas and climate risk premia, underscoring the need for caution in interpreting the results of prior studies.

detail.title: Cross-Jurisdictional Machine Predictions in Antitrust
detail.abstract: Can machine learning models trained to detect collusion in one jurisdiction reliably identify it in entirely different institutional environments? We address this question using procurement auction data from seven jurisdictions - Brazil, Finland, Japan, Sweden, Switzerland, and two US states - and develop bidder-level screens that capture persistent strategic coordination across multiple procurement auctions. Employing ensemble learning with leave-one-jurisdiction-out validation, we find systematic heterogeneity in cross-jurisdictional transferability: performance is high for institutionally comparable markets but deteriorates when procurement rules, contract types, or market structure diverge. Using explainable AI techniques, we show that distributional screens are the most robust and transferable predictors within homogeneous institutional environments, while simpler dispersion measures dominate when procurement regimes diverge. Our findings suggest that algorithmic cartel screening can expand enforcement capacity beyond resource-constrained agencies, but transferability is institutionally bounded - effective deployment requires jurisdiction-specific validation.

title: A Return-to-Work Likelihood Profile: A Transparent Evidence-Based Framework for Describing Work Participation Risk in Compensable Populations

It complies with the confidentiality requirements of the Australian Psychological Society, the Australian Code for the Responsible Conduct of Research and the Privacy Act legislation.
declarations.funderStatement: Nil

detail.abstract: Return to work within compensable populations is shaped by interacting medical, functional, psychological, and socio-administrative influences, yet translating epidemiological evidence into practical decision support remains challenging. This study introduces a Return-to-Work Likelihood Profile, a transparent evidence-based framework that converts established associations with work participation into an additive log-odds scoring system designed to describe relative likelihood rather than predict individual outcomes. Using data derived from a compensable cohort, component indicators were combined to produce a continuous rating. Descriptive classification properties were examined to illustrate score behaviour and to identify an empirically derived interpretive cutoff. The profile demonstrated moderate discrimination between working and non-working groups, supporting its use as a structured aid to clinical and administrative reasoning. The findings illustrate how population-level evidence can be operationalised into interpretable heuristic tools while maintaining transparency regarding statistical assumptions and limitations.

title: Tax Treaty Interpretation and Tunnel Vision: The Supreme Court of India's American Express Decision
affiliations: Maastricht University, Faculty of Law

detail.title: Tax Treaty Interpretation and Tunnel Vision: The Supreme Court of India's American Express Decision
detail.abstract: The attribution of profits to a permanent establishment is one of the most complex and important subjects in tax treaty interpretation. And yet it remains underdeveloped in case law. The American Express judgement of the Supreme Court of India addresses the issue in barely a couple of paragraphs. In this contribution in Tax Notes International, I address the nuances of the arguments that were never made: how does Article 7(3) interact with Art. 7(2) and with Art. 26(2) of the India-US tax treaty? How do we interpret these according to the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties?

title: Trend Quality and Predictability in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Minute-Level Kalshi Data

detail.title: Trend Quality and Predictability in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Minute-Level Kalshi Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author Clyde Greene has an ownership stake in Asara LLC, which entirely funded this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded entirely by Asara LLC.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether "trend quality"-a drift-per-noise statistic computed from within-market price paths-predicts short-horizon price dynamics and ex-post forecast error in prediction markets. Using a large panel of minute-level Kalshi contract snapshots, we construct the Trend Quality Ratio (TQR), defined as the slope of a linear pre-close price trend normalized by its residual dispersion. In non-zero trend regimes, higher |TQR| is associated with both higher short-horizon directionality (continuation) and lower ex-post forecast error, with statistically significant differences between the top and bottom |TQR| deciles. Because many minute-sampled contracts exhibit zero post-window price change, we report both continuation rates conditional on non-zero movements and a tie-adjusted continuation score that retains zero-change cases. Midrange restrictions highlight the importance of bounded-price effects. Quotebased robustness using midquotes increases coverage in thinly traded contracts and preserves the strong error results, while directionality patterns are weaker and closer to 50% when prices are measured from quotes rather than trades.

title: The Use of Tax Incentives to Attract Foreign Investment to Ukraine: a Solution to the Current Economic Instability

This article analyses the effectiveness of existing tax incentives aimed at developing the Ukrainian economy and contributing to post-war reconstruction. The article details various tax incentives and analyses the activities of international agencies and funds that provide security for such financing. title: The Act of Regenerative Expansion: A Non-Coercive Framework for Distributed Wealth Creation in the Age of AI

detail.title: The Act of Regenerative Expansion: A Non-Coercive Framework for Distributed Wealth Creation in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence is increasingly associated with the concentration of economic value at a scale and speed not previously experienced. Much of the current policy discourse seeks to address this through taxation and redistribution within existing economic structures. This paper presents The Act of Regenerative Expansion, a non-coercive public financial framework that operates in parallel with existing systems. Rather than relying on taxation, it introduces a mechanism through which a small share of capitalized AI-driven economic value is continuously recirculated into a regenerative pool that funds community-led infrastructure and resilience initiatives. Initially applied to AI due to its capacity to rapidly reshape value creation, the framework is designed as a general template that may be adopted and adapted by different jurisdictions according to their own economic and constitutional contexts. The Act establishes conditions for structural visibility, allowing economic expansion and regenerative capacity to evolve in balance while preserving free markets and individual sovereignty.

title: Sudan: The Contested Host State
affiliations: Al-Neelain University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Sudan: The Contested Host State

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am the author and the subject is of great interest to my country
